Programming Languages.summary: The security guarantees of existing formally verified compilers for compartmentalized programs in unsafe languages like C stop at a rather high level, assuming a built-in protection mechanism and a block-based memory model. Verifying a concrete, low-level enforcement mechanism for compartment isolation is still a major challenge for current proof techniques. In particular, Abate et al.'s proof technique fails because one of their proof steps, recomposition, essentially requires hiding all information about the code of each compartment, which is not practically achievable at a low level. We propose an extension of their proof technique to a low-level setting where compartments can fully observe each other's code. To do so, we introduce an overlay semantics that allows us to characterize these observations as a form of undefined behaviour, and we use a novel variant of recomposition that we call blame-aware recomposition, which essentially allows recomposing executions as needed in the original high-level proof technique, even if the low-level context observes the code, because this context is ultimately going to be discarded. We apply this new proof to a compartment isolation mechanism that uses a programmable tag-based reference monitor.

Programming Languages.title: Instrumentation Optimization for Practical Dynamic Race Detection
Programming Languages.summary: Dynamic data race detectors are successful at flagging concurrency bugs, but their high runtime overhead limits adoption. This overhead stems primarily from pervasive instrumentation of memory accesses -- a significant fraction of which is for safe accesses. We address this inefficiency through a compiler-integrated approach that identifies safe accesses using static analysis and eliminates instrumentation for these. We strike a careful balance between analysis precision and cost, to ensure applicability to real-world applications. We show that our optimizations never cause ThreadSanitizer to miss races it would otherwise detect. We further observe that many checks are redundant: They only flag a race if a preceding check has already flagged an equivalent race for the same memory location. We show that, when reporting one representative per class is sufficient, even more instrumentation can be eliminated. Lastly, we introduce a dynamic technique that skips instrumentation when there is only one thread at runtime, even when this could not be determined statically. We integrate these static analyses and program transformations into the ThreadSanitizer race detector based on LLVM. Our experiments on a diverse suite of real-world applications, including Memcached, Redis, SQLite, MySQL, and Chromium, demonstrate that our optimizations reduce the number of instrumentation calls at runtime by up to 91% and yield application-level speedups of up to 1.91x, a geometric-mean Chromium speedup of 1.25x on Blink and 1.14x on Speedometer 3.0, and peak speedups reaching 2.28x on Memcached with two server threads. Our optimizations are in the process of being upstreamed into ThreadSanitizer.
Programming Languages.comment: v2: camera-ready version, to appear in the 2026 ACM SIGOPS Annual Technical Conference (SIGOPS ATC 2026). New title; the supplementary material is included as appendices. 24 pages

Programming Languages.title: A Taxonomy of Predicate Transformer Monads for Specifying Monadic Programs
Programming Languages.summary: Monads of weakest precondition predicate transformers are the foundation of several verification frameworks for monadic programs. For specifying monadic computations with nondeterminism and nontermination, in addition to weakest preconditions, we introduce the first strongest postcondition monads covering all combinations of angelic or demonic nondeterminism and partial or total interpretations of nontermination. For extending these base strongest postcondition monads with side effects such as mutable state, monad transformers do not yield the expected monads, so we instead generalize the base monads to arrows and use arrow transformers. We give a taxonomy of weakest precondition and strongest postcondition monads, for the base monads and for their versions with state, and show that the known relationships between under- and over-approximate triples based on predicate transformers already hold at the level of the predicate transformers themselves. We use the predicate transformer monads to define under- and over-approximate triples and, where possible, Dijkstra monads. Finally, we relate these two specification styles.
Programming Languages.comment: Submitted to ESOP'27, in v2 same PDF but fixed author order in metadata

Programming Languages.title: Compiling Environment Classifiers to Contextual Modal Types
Programming Languages.summary: Type systems for metaprogramming take one of two approaches to safeguarding the scopes of variables in generated code. They either use Environment Classifiers (EC) to identify scopes by name (Taha and Nielsen, 2003), or they use Contextual Modal Type Theory (CMTT) to match scopes by structure (Nanevski, Pfenning, and Pientka, 2008). In this paper, we connect these two approaches by compiling a calculus with polymorphic environment classifiers, subtyping, and mutable references to a CMTT-based calculus with polymorphic contexts, mutable references, and first-class substitutions. The key idea is to map each environment classifier to a context. We prove that the compilation preserves types and that compilation preserves the behavior of metaprograms. Both proofs are mechanized in Agda. The compilation shows that CMTT is at least as expressive as environment classifiers. We conjecture that the converse compilation is difficult, because environment classifiers impose a stricter regime on the metaprogram.
Programming Languages.comment: 45 pages, 26 figures

Programming Languages.title: Forall-Exists Relational Verification by Filtering to Forall-Forall
Programming Languages.summary: Relational verification encompasses reasoning about data abstraction, security and privacy, secure compilation, and functional specification of tensor programs, among others. Several relational logics and tools support compositional reasoning about $\forall\forall$ (2-safety) properties and, generally, $k$-safety properties. In contrast, few logics and tools exist for reasoning about $\forall\exists$ properties which are critical in the presence of nondeterminism. This paper's primary contribution is a technique for verifying a $\forall\exists$ judgment by way of a novel transformation. The filter-adequacy transformation adds assertions to a product program in such a way that the desired $\forall\exists$ property (of a pair of underlying unary programs) is implied by a $\forall\forall$ property of the transformed product. The paper develops bicoms, a form of product programs that facilitates expressing good alignments and caters for direct translation of $\forall\forall$ properties to unary correctness; proves that successful $\forall\forall$ verification of a transformed bicom implies the $\forall\exists$ spec for its underlying unary commands; and evaluates the technique using a prototype auto-active relational verifier. The technique enables users to work with ordinary assertions and assumptions, and a standard assertion language, so that existing $\forall\forall$ and unary verification tools can be used for $\forall\exists$.
Programming Languages.comment: v2: expanded evaluation section; expository improvements throughout

Programming Languages.title: Verified Purely Functional Catenable Real-Time Deques
Programming Languages.summary: We present OCaml and Rocq implementations of Kaplan and Tarjan's purely functional, real-time catenable deques. The correctness of our Rocq code is machine-checked.

Programming Languages.title: Runtime Semantic Discovery for Evolving Action Alphabets
Programming Languages.summary:
Runtime Verification typically assumes a fixed alphabet of observable actions. This assumption becomes fragile in evolving software systems, where updates, reconfigurations, or architectural changes may rename, split, or fuse actions while preserving the system's high-level intent. In these cases, previously valid monitors and specifications may become misaligned with the running system.
  In this paper, we study runtime semantic discovery, namely the problem of identifying whether newly observed actions play the same operational role as previously known ones, without reconstructing a global behavioral model. To this end, we propose a local and runtime-computable notion of action similarity based on the neighbor contexts in which actions occur within execution traces. We define a family of k-neighbor equivalences and use them to compare systems whose observable alphabets differ.
  Our approach is intentionally lightweight: it does not aim to fully characterize behavioral preservation, but rather to identify candidate semantic correspondences between actions in evolving systems. We discuss the expressive power and limitations of neighbor-based equivalence and show how inferred correspondences can support the adaptation of runtime monitors and specifications under selected classes of alphabet evolution.
Programming Languages.comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Version presented at the VORTEX 2026 workshop (co-located with ECOOP 2026)

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Matrix-Vector Complexity of Low-Rank Approximation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We establish matching polynomial query bounds for low-rank approximation from exact matrix--vector products. Given an unknown matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, at each step a randomized algorithm chooses either $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and receives $Av$, or $u\in\mathbb{R}^m$ and receives $A^\top u$. The choice may depend measurably on all previous queries and replies and on the algorithm's private randomness; each vector product costs one query. The output is a rank-$k$ right projector with Schatten-$p$ residual at most $1+\varepsilon$ times optimal. Write $N=\min\{m,n\}$ and let $Q_p^*$ denote the worst-case query budget for success probability $2/3$ on every input. For every $1\le k<N$ and sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, our lower bounds, combined with existing Krylov upper bounds, give $Q_p^*=\widetildeΘ\!\left(\min\{N,k\min\{p^{1/6}\varepsilon^{-1/3},\varepsilon^{-1/2}\}\}\right)$ $(2\le p<\infty)$, $Q_\infty^*=\widetildeΘ\!\left(\min\{N,k\varepsilon^{-1/2}\}\right)$. These bounds have universal constants and allow $p$ to vary with the problem parameters, identifying the transition at $p\varepsilon\asymp1$. A complementary result for each fixed $1\le p<2$ gives $\widetildeΘ_p(\min\{N,k\varepsilon^{-1/3}\})$, with constants and an accuracy threshold that may depend on $p$. Together, the results recover this fixed-norm rate for every fixed finite $p$, supplying the multiplicative rank dependence missing from previous lower bounds. Tildes suppress logarithmic factors. The proof extends adaptive Wishart deferred decisions to a rectangular factor with a $k$-dimensional nullspace. Posterior overlap gives a short fixed-norm argument, while persistence of small compression eigenvalues controls growing $p$ and the spectral endpoint. Exact range recovery handles target costs of order $k$; the Wishart family covers the remaining regimes.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A simplified proof of the FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a simplified, self-contained proof of OpenAI's FPRAS for counting perfect matchings in general graphs. As in the original proof, we use a restricted Poincaré inequality for two matchings to sample weighted perfect matchings and estimate their total weight. We simplify the proof of this inequality by isolating parts of alternating cycles directly on the original vertex set and controlling the resulting error terms. This avoids the auxiliary vertices and tree constructions used in the original proof. The argument preserves the required parameter bounds and yields the same FPRAS guarantee.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Randomized Matvec Lower Bounds for Simplex-Based Matrix Games
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We prove randomized matrix-vector query lower bounds for two normalized matrix-game geometries: a Euclidean unit ball against a probability simplex, with row norms at most one, and two probability simplices, with entries of absolute value at most one. Each query returns $(Ax,A^\top y)$ for arbitrary real vectors. The algorithm must return a feasible pair with full saddle-point gap at most $\varepsilon$, with probability at least $2/3$ on every admissible matrix. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, the worst-case query complexities are $Ω(\varepsilon^{-2/3}/(\log^2(1/\varepsilon)\log\log(1/\varepsilon)))$ for ball-simplex games and $Ω(\varepsilon^{-2/3}/(\log^{7/3}(1/\varepsilon)\log\log(1/\varepsilon)))$ for simplex-simplex games. The hard instances have dimensions of order $\varepsilon^{-2/3}$ and $\varepsilon^{-2/3}/\log^{1/3}(1/\varepsilon)$, respectively, and the bounds extend to larger dimensions. These lower bounds match the deterministic upper bounds of Karmarkar, O'Carroll, and Sidford up to logarithmic factors. The proof extracts a fresh Gaussian core after adaptive two-sided queries and uses uncertainty in its smallest singular value to establish linear-system solve hardness. Two reductions transfer this hardness to matrix games by converting a small full gap into a small residual, with an additional logarithmic normalization loss only for simplex-simplex games.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Tight Oracle Threshold for \(k\)-Submodular Maximization
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We prove that, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), a \((\frac{k}{2k-1}+\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithm for maximizing monotone \(k\)-submodular functions requires exponentially many value-oracle queries. This improves the \(\frac{k+1}{2k}\) oracle bound of Iwata, Tanigawa, and Yoshida. Their \(\frac{k}{2k-1}\)-approximation algorithm therefore gives the exact threshold in the monotone setting. For \(k\ge5\), our bound also matches, up to an arbitrarily small loss, Aggarwal's recent approximation guarantee for
  non-monotone \(k\)-submodular maximization.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved exploration of temporal graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A temporal graph $G$ is a sequence $(G_t)_{t \in I}$ of graphs on the same vertex set of size $n$. The \emph{temporal exploration problem} asks for the length of the shortest sequence of vertices that starts at a given vertex, visits every vertex, and at each time step $t$ either stays at the current vertex or moves to an adjacent vertex in $G_t$. When each $G_t$ is connected and has bounded maximum degree, Erlebach, Kammer, Luo, Sajenko, and Spooner [ICALP 2019] showed that an exploration exists in $\mathcal{O}(n^{7/4})$ time steps.
  We significantly improve this bound by showing that $\mathcal{O}(n^{3/2}\sqrt{\log n})$ time steps suffice. In fact, we prove a more general statement unifying this setting with many others. Let the \emph{average temporal maximum degree} $D$ of $G$ be the average of $\max_{t \in I}d_{G_t}(v)$ over all vertices $v \in V(G)$, where $d_{G_t}(v)$ denotes the degree of $v$ in $G_t$. We show that if each $G_t$ is connected, then an exploration exists in $\mathcal{O}(n^{3/2}\sqrt{D\log n})$ time steps. This gives the first subquadratic upper bound when the underlying graph has bounded average degree, improving the previous best bounds when it is planar or has bounded treewidth. Our bound is subquadratic already when $D=o(n/\log n)$.
  In addition, we make progress on a recent conjecture of Baguley, Göbel, Klodt, Skretas, Sylvester, and Zamaraev [SODA 2025]. They conjectured that if $μ$ is a probability distribution on trees with maximum degree at most $Δ$ and each $G_t$ is sampled independently from $μ$, then an exploration exists in $\mathcal{O}(\sqrtΔn)$ time steps with high probability. We show that there is a temporal exploration of length $\mathcal{O}(Δn\log^3 n)$ with high probability. This improves the previous best bound of $\mathcal{O}(n^{3/2})$ and extends to the more general setup of average temporal maximum degree.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Capacitated Line Aggregation with Maximum Delay
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study capacitated line aggregation with per-batch maximum delay. Requests arrive over time at locations on a rooted half-line and are served in instantaneous batches of at most $k$ requests. Each batch pays the distance to its farthest request plus the waiting time of its oldest request. The objective is to minimize the total cost.
  We give a deterministic online algorithm with competitive ratio $36+12\sqrt3$. The algorithm uses a Next Fit idea along paths of nested time intervals: it assigns a new group to an existing batch when a path-load test permits, and opens a new batch otherwise. The path load controls both capacity and the cost of opening new batches. Randomizing the common scale improves the expected competitive ratio to $(18+6\sqrt3)/\ln2$ against an oblivious adversary. Both guarantees extend to arbitrary indivisible request sizes.
  We also study capacitated LAD in the learning-augmented model. Advice revealed at its service times allows $(1+ε)$-consistency against every complete feasible advice schedule and $O(ε^{-2})$-robustness. The analysis charges repeated switches to successive decreases in the remaining advice cost.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Orienting mixed graphs for reachability pairs: When the all pairs setting is easier than the general one
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Given a mixed graph $G$ and an ordered pair $(u,v)$ of vertices in $V(G)$, we say that an orientation $\vec{G}$ of $G$ satisfies $(u,v)$ if $v$ is reachable from $u$ in $\vec{G}$. We consider problems in which we seek orientations that satisfy a maximum number of pairs. We distinguish between two different problems. In the most general problem called Fixed Pairs Maximum Mixed Reachability Orientation (FPRO), a multiset $P$ of ordered pairs of vertices in $V(G)$ comes with the input. In the more restricted problem All Pairs Maximum Mixed Reachability Orientation (APRO), $P$ contains exactly one copy of every ordered pair of distinct vertices in $V(G)$. We compare the computational complexity of FPRO and APRO in two ways: First, we show that both FPRO and APRO behave similarly when it comes to approximation. Namely, they both admit an asymptotic approximation, but are unlikely to admit a constant factor approximation. Then, we consider the parameterization with respect to the treewidth of the underlying graph of the input mixed graph. We show that here the complexities of FPRO and APRO differ significantly. While it is well-known that FPRO is NP-hard even when this parameter is 1, we show that APRO is XP with respect to this parameter. On the other hand, we give a $W[1]$-hardness result for APRO.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Constructive Arithmetic Regularity for Abelian Groups
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The arithmetic regularity lemma of Green is a fundamental tool in additive combinatorics, providing a decomposition of arbitrary subsets of finite Abelian groups into pseudorandom pieces with respect to Fourier analysis. Over the years, it has found numerous applications in combinatorics, property testing, and theoretical computer science. However, Green's proof is existential, and many algorithmic applications require an efficient procedure for constructing the underlying regular decomposition. De, Nadimpalli, and Servedio (SODA 2022) developed a query-efficient constructive regularity framework over $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and explicitly raised the problem of extending their dimension-independent sumset-estimation algorithm to other finite Abelian groups.
  In this work, we resolve this question for finite Abelian groups of constant torsion. We develop the first constructive version of Green's {\em Arithmetic Regularity Lemma} in this general setting. Given oracle access to a subset of the group, our algorithm computes an implicit description of a regular decomposition together with an oracle representation of a structured subset satisfying the guarantees of Green's lemma. The algorithm runs in time and query complexity polynomial in the regularity parameters and the tower bound, while remaining independent of the size of the ambient group.
  As applications, we obtain efficient algorithms for removing linear configurations and approximately counting linear images, including weighted sumsets and suitable matrix systems of Cauchy--Schwarz complexity one, over finite Abelian groups of constant torsion. Our results provide a unified algorithmic framework extending dimension-independent constructive arithmetic regularity and its applications beyond $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Ski Rental with Uniform Stochastic Signals
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Ski rental is one of the most fundamental online problems, where an agent repeatedly decides whether it should continue renting for a service, or buy it at a one-time fixed cost. In classic online analysis, an adversary may freely select any arbitrary time horizon $t$ after which the instance terminates, hence leading to strong competitive ratio lower bounds of 2 (deterministic) and $e/(e-1)$ (randomized).
  We consider a novel but natural model aiming at limiting the adversary's power without degrading its flexibility. A stochastic signal, containing no information apart from its arrival time, is transmitted to the algorithm at a time drawn from a known distribution scaled to $[0,t]$. This framework allows us to account for visible effects of the adversary's choice to the algorithm. Focusing as a first step on uniform distributions, we show that the best possible competitive ratios are approximately $1.478$ (deterministic) and $1.438$ (randomized). Surprisingly, simplistic deterministic strategies already achieve a performance of $1.489$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Dynamic $(Δ+1)$-Coloring Against an Adaptive Adversary: Faster, Simpler, Worst-Case, and Bounded Recourse
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study fully dynamic $(Δ+1)$-coloring against an adaptive adversary. Behnezhad, Rajaraman, and Wasim (SODA 2025) gave the first algorithm with $\tilde O(n^{8/9})$ amortized update time, later improved to $\tilde O(n^{2/3})$ by Flin and Halldórsson (ICALP 2025). We give a fully dynamic $(Δ+1)$-coloring algorithm with $\tilde O(\sqrt n)$ \textbf{worst-case} update time. Unlike previous algorithms, it avoids sparse-dense decompositions and relies only on elementary data structures, resulting in a short self-contained algorithm and analysis. Moreover, it avoids global recoloring, resulting in a worst-case recourse of $3$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Constructive FPT Algorithm for Integer Cone Optimization with Convex Costs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a deterministic fixed-parameter algorithm for integer cone optimization with convex costs. Given $τ$ rational polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^d$, each with a convex cost function, we minimize the total cost of nonnegative integer combinations of their lattice points subject to arbitrary rational linear constraints on the typewise aggregates and generator counts. Our algorithm runs in time \[
  2^{τ\log(τ+1)\,2^{O(d)}}\cdot |I|^{O(1)}, \] where $|I|$ is the total binary input length. It constructs an optimal representation using at most $2^{2d+1}$ distinct generators per type.
  For a single generator type, the running time becomes $2^{2^{O(d)}}\cdot |I|^{O(1)}$. This yields constructive FPT algorithms for Cone and Polytope Intersection and high-multiplicity bin packing, improving the $2^{2^{O(d\log d)}}\cdot |I|^{O(1)}$ bound of Koana and Kumabe (2026) for bin-packing decision. The dependence on $d$ is ETH-tight for point-in-cone, high-multiplicity bin packing, and vector bin packing. For vector bin packing, this establishes fixed-parameter tractability in the number of item types. We also obtain new FPT parameterizations for high-multiplicity scheduling on uniform and unrelated machines: makespan minimization and $\ell_q$-load minimization are FPT in the number of job and machine types.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Solving Classes of Linear Programs with Strongly Polynomial Straight Line Complexity in Strongly Polynomial Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Recently, Allamigeon, Dadush, Loho, Natura, and Végh (ADLNV, SICOMP 2025) introduced an interior point method for linear programs whose number of iterations is bounded by the so-called straight line complexity (SLC) of the instance. This yields a strongly polynomial bound on the number of iterations of the corresponding interior point algorithm for broad classes of linear programs. In particular, in the companion paper we give a strongly polynomial straight line complexity bound for two-variable-per-inequality linear programs. However, in order to obtain a strongly polynomial algorithm for these classes, one also needs to address two important technical issues: initialization and bit-complexity bounds. Standard IPM initialization techniques either require numerical estimates that cannot be obtained in the strongly polynomial model, or involve modifying the instance in ways that do not preserve the geometry of the original LP, potentially affecting the SLC.
  In this work, we present an initialization framework for interior point methods for linear programming, along with a rounding procedure that ensures the continued feasibility of the IPM. We develop a multistage scheme in which each stage can be initialized in strongly polynomial time given the output of the previous stage. Additionally, we address the challenge of controlling the bit complexity of each iterate throughout the algorithm. To this end, we show that it is possible to represent iterates as low-complexity convex combinations of vertices and extreme rays. Our combinatorial rounding step is independent of the algorithm in ADLNV 2025, and can be applied more broadly in the context of path-following methods.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: This paper is based on the STOC 2024 proceedings paper "A strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or column'' , and includes the full details of the initialization framework and the bit complexity arguments

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Output-linear time enumeration of potential maximal cliques
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
First defined by Bouchitté and Todinca, Potential Maximal Cliques (PMC) are a well studied notion in graph theory due to its numerous applications. The PMCs of an undirected graph $G$ are defined as the maximal cliques of the minimal triangulations of $G$. Their number can be exponential in the size of the graph. PMCs were crucial in the design of a polynomial-time algorithm which solves Maximum Weight Independent Set on $P_6$-free graphs (Grzesik, Klimošová, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, 2020). They also play a central role in the proposal of a polynomial-time algorithm to solve Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ (Fomin, Todinca, Villanger, 2013).
  Last but not least, certainly one of the main application of PMCs is the existence of an exact dynamic-programming algorithm to determine the treewidth of a graph (Fomin, Kratsch, Todinca, Villanger, 2008) which uses its list of PMCs as an input. In fact, the enumeration of PMCs stands as the bottleneck for the computation of treewidth with this method: the PMC-enumeration step takes output-quadratic time (Bouchitté, Todinca, 2002) while the dynamic-programming one takes a time linear in the number of PMCs. This two-step procedure was proven to be among the most performing approaches in practice to determine treewidth.
  Answering a longstanding open question, we propose an algorithm to enumerate PMCs in output-linear time, i.e. a running time linear in the number of PMCs. This offers nice perspectives not only from the theoretical viewpoint - better running time for the PMC-based methods determining treewidth, for Minimum Fill-In and Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ - but also from the practical side, with the possibility to propose top-performance implementation.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: This paper was accepted at SODA 2027. 54 pages, 18 figures

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Internalizing Chain-of-thought into Looped Transformers
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) enables constant-bit-size transformers to perform general-purpose computation through generated tokens (Li and Wang, 2025a), whereas looped transformers carry out the same computation by recurrence in hidden states (latent thought). We construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between CoT and latent thought. For a prescribed loop count $L=L(n)$ and a fixed integer $k\ge1$ satisfying $s(n)^{1/k}=Ω(L)$, our transformer simulates a time-$t(n)$, space-$s(n)$ Turing machine using a context window of $O(s(n)/L)$ and $O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}/L)$ generated tokens, reducing both resources by a factor of $L$ relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation. The construction also holds with softmax attention at constant bit-size, under the finite-precision kernel specified in this paper.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Integer Programing: An Algorithm with Exponent Linear in the Dimension
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study integer programs in standard form $\min\{\mathbf{c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x}:A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},\ \mathbf{l}\leq\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{u},\ \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^n\}$, where $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{d\times n}$ and all entries of $\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{l},\mathbf{u}$ are integers. Let $N$ be an upper bound on the absolute values of the entries of $A$. We give a deterministic algorithm running in time \[
  \operatorname{poly}(L_{\rm in})+
  f(d)\,N^{O(d)}\bigl(1+\log(c_{\max}+1)\bigr)^{O(1)}, \] where $c_{\max}$ bounds the absolute values of the costs and $L_{\rm in}$ is the input length. Prior to our work, the best known running time was $N^{O(d^2)}$ [Eisenbrand \& Weismantel'20], and it has been a fundamental open problem whether the exponent $O(d^2)$ can be improved to one linear in $d$. We answer this question affirmatively.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Graph determination problem from knowledge of its subgraphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In the context of graph reconstruction studies, this paper addresses the problem defined as follows: given a sample of vertex-coloured graphs, each associated with a number, does there exist a connected graph containing exactly the given number of induced subgraphs isomorphic to each graph in the sample, such that every edge of the solution graph is included in at least one of these subgraphs. This paper first shows that this problem is $Σ$______-complete. The associated optimisation problem is to determine the minimum number of vertices in a solution graph, if one exists. For instances consisting of two paths, we prove NP-completeness in general and give a polynomial-time dynamic programming algorithm when one path is monochromatic.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Exact minimum Birkhoff decompositions of doubly stochastic matrices with finite precision
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The minimum Birkhoff decomposition problem asks for a representation of a doubly stochastic matrix as a convex combination of as few permutation matrices as possible. This NP-hard problem arises in the scheduling of switches in data centers and satellite systems, in random assignments in economics and in the statistics of rankings. We consider doubly stochastic matrices whose entries are given with a fixed number of decimal digits and look for exact decompositions whose weights have the same precision. We propose a parallel method with three parts. For matrices built from few permutation matrices, the first part reads the weights from the frequencies of the entries and places them on the matrix positions by a rule that, given the correct weights, never fixes a position wrongly. The second part computes lower bounds from pairs of rows or columns, which remain valid for real weights, and from certificates of a satisfiability solver. For matrices built from many permutation matrices, the third part runs a beam search over steps that each make at least one entry zero. On 375 test instances with up to 100 rows, the method proves optimality for 208 instances, and 197 of these proofs also hold for real weights. Of the 190 instances built from few permutation matrices, 187 are solved to proven optimality, 180 of them within one second. Compared with the best exact decompositions known before, the new decompositions are shorter for 278 instances and never longer.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Hadamard Transforms for Dimension Reduction
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Using the Hadamard matrix for dimension reduction can accelerate the computation due to the fast Hadamard transform. However, the previous target dimension bounds in terms of the Gaussian width depend on the ambient dimension. In this paper, we obtain the following ambient dimension free bound using three Hadamard-diagonal blocks. Let $H\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be the normalized Walsh-Hadamard matrix, and let $D_1,D_2,D_3\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be independent Rademacher diagonal matrices. We prove that for any symmetric set $T\subset \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, \[ \mathbb P\left\{\sup_{\boldsymbol t\in T}\big|\frac dm\|P_ΩHD_3HD_2HD_1\boldsymbol t\|_2^2-1\big|\le\varepsilon\right\} \ge1-δ\] whenever \[ m\gtrsim\varepsilon^{-2}w(T)^2\log^2\frac eδ\,\log^4\!\left(e+\frac{w(T)}\varepsilon\log\frac eδ\right). \] Here $w(T)$ is the Gaussian width of $T$, and $Ω$ is a set of $m$ distinct coordinates chosen uniformly. This is the first ambient dimension free bound on the target dimension using Hadamard transforms, for an arbitrary symmetric set in terms of its Gaussian width.
  We also prove that it is impossible to obtain an ambient dimension free bound for an arbitrary set in terms of its Gaussian width using two Hadamard-diagonal blocks.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: On the Role of Normalization in Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding for 1-bit Compressed Sensing
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding (BIHT) is a simple, yet effective, greedy method for recovering a sparse vector from one-bit sign measurements. In its original form, BIHT performs a ``gradient-descent'' step, followed by hard thresholding. A convergence analysis of this algorithm was left open in the introductory work of Jacques, Laska, Boufounos, and Baraniuk [IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory (2013)] and has remained unresolved for over a decade, with subsequent sharp analyses studying a {\em normalized variant} instead, that additionally projects every iterate onto the unit sphere. This paper resolves that gap and characterizes when per-iteration normalization is algorithmically necessary. In the noiseless setting, we prove a universal, sample-optimal convergence theorem for the original BIHT algorithm. Specifically, with $\widetilde O(s/ε)$ measurements, a deterministic, computable finite-time iterate has directional error at most $ε$, simultaneously for every $s$-sparse unit vector. This matches the optimal sample dependence achieved by normalized BIHT in prior work. Under sign corruptions, we prove a sharp separation. If at most a $τ$ fraction of signs are flipped adversarially, then BIHT, without per-iterate normalization, still reaches the robust error floor at an early iterate with a matching $\widetilde O(s/ε)$ sample complexity rate as its normalized variant. This recovery, however, is not stable. We prove a scalar lower bound showing that any nontrivial corruption pattern, even one that involves only one flipped sign together with one clean sign, forces the iterates to oscillate indefinitely. Consequently, no general last-iterate convergence theorem can hold for BIHT under sign corruptions, while its normalized surrogate provably escapes this instance.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Communication Complexity of Universal Features
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Motivated by the notion of features from machine learning, we study the complexity of representing data that allows for evaluation with a given family of functions. Concretely, we consider a deterministic encoder that observes $X\sim D$ and produces a finite encoding before a task $f\in\mathcal{F}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}}$ is specified. For each task, a decoder must predict $f(X)$ with error at most $\varepsilon$ under $D$. We construct an encoder that outputs a representation with $O(d^{*}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ bits, where $d^{*}$ is the dual VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. Our encoder greedily selects $O((d^{*}/\varepsilon)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ functions from the class and uses their joint label pattern to produce the encoding. The key idea in our upper bound is a novel potential function argument, where we compare the entropy gained from each greedy selection with the number of patterns allowed by the dual VC dimension. We present lower bounds showing that the representation length achieved by our encoder is worst-case optimal for every $d^* \ge 1$ and $\varepsilon < 1/4$ up to a universal constant factor, and instance-wise optimal for every family $\mathcal{F}$ up to an $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ factor. We give two ways to learn the representation from unlabeled samples, with different guarantees on the representation size and sample complexity. Experimentally, we verify the greedy construction's accuracy-size tradeoff and explore its connection to neural sparse autoencoders.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Simpler Logarithmic Approximation Algorithms for the Optimal Decision Tree and Adaptive Set Cover
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the problem of constructing a decision tree that identifies an unknown hypothesis from a given ground set, under both average- and worst-case cost. The Optimal Decision Tree (ODT) problem has been extensively studied in the literature, and $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$-approximation guarantees are known for each criterion, including a simultaneous guarantee for both (here $n$ is the number of hypotheses) [ICML]. Although most of the existing algorithm use simple greedy strategies, their analyses rely on intricate arguments. Since ODT is a fundamental problem with wide-ranging applications, we are interested in developing algorithms that are both effective and easy to understand.
  We present a new greedy algorithm with a simplified analysis that simultaneously achieves approximation factors below $3.65\log_2 n$ for worst-case cost and $7.3\log_2 n$ for average-case cost. Our algorithm for the Optimal Decision Tree behaves greedily with respect to the hereby introduced Separating Subfamily problem which asks for the cheapest subfamily of tests which partitions the hypotheses into pieces of small enough size. We show that the Separating Subfamily can itself be reduced to an instance of the well-known Maximum Coverage problem. At the core of our approach lies exploiting properties of cutting a clique into small pieces, where edges represent pairs of hypotheses to be separated. In the spirit of simplicity, we also provide a new and straightforward application of ODT: an $\mathcal{O}(\log (k\cdot n))$-approximation for the Adaptive Set Cover problem, where $k$ is the number of possible realizations.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Parameterizing Cluster Editing by the Number of Deletions
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In Cluster Editing, we are given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$ and ask whether at most $k$ edge insertions and deletions turn $G$ into a disjoint union of cliques. Komusiewicz and Niedermeier asked in 2012 at MFCS whether Cluster Editing is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the number $\ell$ of edge deletions, a parameter based on the solution rather than on the structure of the input graph. We answer this question negatively: Cluster Editing with at most $k$ edits, at most $\ell$ of which are deletions, is W[1]-hard with respect to $\ell$, even when combined with the pathwidth and the feedback edge set number of the input graph. The hardness extends to editing towards $H$-free graphs for every graph $H$ that is a clique minus one edge on at least four vertices. On the positive side, we show that the problem becomes fixed-parameter tractable when $\ell$ is combined with the excess $μ$ of $k$ over the lower bound given by a packing of modification-disjoint induced paths on three vertices, a lower bound that state-of-the-art solvers use. Each of the two parameters alone leads to intractability, but together they admit an $O(4^{μ+\ell}\cdot(n+m+μ))$-time algorithm and a problem kernel with $O((\ell+μ)^2)$ vertices. Both results extend to packings of stars and the algorithm extends to $H$-free editing.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: CAFS: A Cache-Aware Frequency Sort for Low-Cardinality Integer Data on x86-64
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Integer sorts in OLAP engines often run on columns whose cardinality $K$ is much smaller than the array length $N$. After a group-by stage the intermediate key column has $K$ bounded by the number of distinct group keys, and even a column-store scan typically operates on dictionary-encoded categorical fields where $K$ never exceeds a few thousand. A comparison sort on such a column still pays $Θ(N \log N)$ comparisons, and a radix sort still pays $Θ(N \cdot B/b)$ byte passes, irrespective of $K$. This paper describes CAFS, an integer sort that does exploit it on x86-64 with AVX2. The algorithm combines a SIMD bucket sized to one cache line, a Chao1 cardinality estimator over 1024 strided samples (kept in a heap-allocated 40 KB open-addressing table), and an adaptive dispatcher backed by a spill safety guard. The hot loop is branchless and uses AVX2 cmpeq together with movemask and tzcnt to locate the matching lane. We benchmarked CAFS on a full-factorial grid of 58 array sizes $N$ from $10^3$ to $3 \cdot 10^7$ with dense $K$ schedules per $N$, producing 592770 timed runs against pdqsort, IPS4o, vqsort, ska_sort, and std::sort. In the $K \ll N$ band the throughput is 1.7 to 3.1x that of pdqsort, 1.7 to 3.5x IPS4o, and 1.2 to 2.3x vqsort. The operational crossover against pdqsort is at $K \approx 1.3 \cdot 10^5$; against ska_sort, $K \approx 8.14 \cdot 10^5$; against vqsort, $K \approx 6.7 \cdot 10^5$; and against IPS4o the curves only converge near $K = N$. Of the five baselines, only vqsort actually overtakes CAFS once the crossover is passed, which makes the vqsort threshold at $K \approx 6.7 \cdot 10^5$ the binding constraint on the operational range of CAFS.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Connected (Dense) Partition for Tree-Like Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We focus on two variants of graph partitioning problems, connected partition and dense partition. Formally, given a graph $G=(V,E)$ and a partition of its vertices $\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots, P_k\}$ we say that $\mathcal P$ is a connected partition of $G$ if each $P_i$ induces a connected graph in $G$. Many classical variants of this problem impose additional restrictions both on the number of parts as well as on the size of each part. Moreover, given a partition $\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots, P_k\}$ we define its density by $d(\mathcal P):=\sum_{i=1}^k |E(P_i)|/|V(P_i)|$. The problem Maximum Dense Graph Partition asks to construct a partition of maximum density. We study this problem both with and without fixed number of sets $k$. We prove the following results:
  1. A polynomial time algorithm for \textsc{Maximum Dense Graph Partition} of thick forests, a subclass of chordal graphs, generalizing the previously known polynomial time algorithm on block graphs.
  2. A generic dynamic programming algorithm to construct (if possible) a connected partition into $k$ sets of prescribed sizes on graphs with bounded treewidth. This yields algorithms for both variants of Dense Graph Partition and an efficient construction for the Győri-Lovász theorem.
  3. The $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness of Maximum Dense Graph Partition restricted to split graphs, showing that thick trees are a boundary for the polynomial computability of this problem.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Deterministic Shift Equivalence Testing for Sparse Polynomials
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the shift equivalence testing problem for high-degree sparse multivariate polynomials. Given explicit spar se representations of two polynomials $f,g\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, with exponents encoded in binary, sparsities $s$ and $t$, and total degree at most $d$, the task is to decide whether there is a vector $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ such that $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{a})\equiv g(\mathbf{x})$. Furthermore, one needs to output such a vector if it exists. Dvir, Oliveira, and Shpilka (ICALP 2014) studied shift equivalence for low-degree arithmetic circuits. Their framew ork does not apply directly to sparse polynomials, which are not closed under shifts, and they left open whether shift equivalence of sparse polynomials admits an efficient deterministic algorithm.
  We answer this question positively over $\mathbb{Q}$. If the input coefficients have bit-size at most $τ$, we sh ow that a rational shift of polynomial bit-size exists whenever the polynomials are shift equivalent. Moreover, our alg orithm outputs such a shift and has a running time of $\operatorname{poly}(n,s,t,τ,\log d)$ in the bit model. The ar ithmetic and structural parts of our result also hold over any field of characteristic zero or characteristic larger th an $d$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Verified Purely Functional Catenable Real-Time Deques
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We present OCaml and Rocq implementations of Kaplan and Tarjan's purely functional, real-time catenable deques. The correctness of our Rocq code is machine-checked.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Short Note on Algorithms For The Noisy $k$-XOR Problem
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: This mostly expository note studies the sample-noise regimes in which the testing problem for noisy $k$-XOR in dimension $n$ can be efficiently solved. Concretely, we ask what pairs $(β, δ)$ admit algorithms running in time $n^{O(k)}$ where $m = n^β, β\in [0,k]$ is the number of samples and $\mathsf{Bern}(n^{-δ}),δ\in (0,+\infty)$ is the noise distribution. The current state-of-the-art algorithms are: I. A folklore algorithm when $β> 1, δ>1$ based on Gaussian elimination; II. A folklore algorithm when $β\ge k/2$ based on the birthday paradox; III. A recent algorithm in the regime $β> δ+ k(1-δ), δ\in (0,1)$ based on a reduction to the first algorithm [DJ24,CSZ24]. IV. Extending [AF09], we strictly improve the last regime to $β> δ+ (k-1)(1-δ), δ\in (0,1).$ These algorithms correspond to efficiently finding short cycles in uniform hypergraphs and can be equivalently phrased as algorithmic Moore bounds.

Graphics.title: Can It Actually Work? Synthesizing Functional CAD Mechanisms
Graphics.summary: While LLM agents can generate visually plausible CAD assemblies, these designs often fail to fulfill their intended physical functions. We study functional CAD design, a setting where agents interpret underspecified requests to construct and iteratively revise mechanisms that satisfy functional requirements in physical simulation. Verifying these requirements is nontrivial: different candidate mechanisms may realize the same function through entirely different components, controls, and operating sequences. To bridge this gap, we propose FunCAD-Harness, a framework that translates abstract requirements into candidate-specific physical tests and uses simulation feedback to guide design revisions. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce FunCADBench, a benchmark spanning 46 mechanism families with interdependent and multi-step operations. Experiments across frontier LLM agents show that FunCAD-Harness exposes subtle mechanical failures invisible to visual inspection, substantially improving functional success rates over standard simulation-augmented baselines. Ultimately, our work marks a step toward CAD agents capable of translating human intent into working mechanisms.

Graphics.title: Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer
Graphics.summary: A geometric style learned from one family of shapes is typically applied to new shapes from the same family. We consider a more challenging setting: learning the geometric design language of a stylized Latin alphabet and applying it to new forms, from Greek glyphs to entirely different structures such as human poses. We introduce Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed. This setting is deceptively challenging: the difficulty is not merely learning a style, but learning the style without learning the shape family in which it was observed. We represent target forms by structural sketches and disentangle structural adherence from style realization using a Geometry LoRA and a style-specific LoRA. Critically, open-form transfer requires the Geometry LoRA to be universal. To achieve this, we devise a geometry-enrichment strategy that constructs a large and purposefully diverse collection of synthetic structural sketches spanning a broad range of unfamiliar geometries. Our experiments and ablations demonstrate the importance of both disentanglement and this universal geometry prior, enabling geometric styles learned from glyphs, pictograms, and other shape families to be transferred to substantially different, unseen forms.

Graphics.title: RoboCloth: A Large-Scale Real Cloth Material Dataset for Neural Reflectance Reconstruction
Graphics.summary: We present RoboCloth, a dataset of 500 real cloth materials captured under flexible, calibrated camera and lighting configurations, where both are robotically controlled during acquisition. Each material is imaged in approximately 580 high-dynamic range frames spanning a wide view-light hemisphere; camera poses are refined via structure-from-motion and aligned to the robot frame, yielding per-material sparse surface geometry and structured per-point reflectance observations ready for neural material training. We demonstrate the value of this data through a two-stage neural reconstruction pipeline: Stage 1 trains a shared MLP decoder on our corpus to learn cloth material priors; Stage 2 then freezes the decoder and fits a dense 2048x2048 latent texture to each target material. Evaluating on held-out materials from our own dataset and on the independent UBO2014 benchmark, we show that a decoder trained on our captures outperforms decoders trained on existing measured reflectance datasets and analytic PBR fitting, transferring to unseen acquisition systems without modification. The dataset, calibration files, observation tensors, and train/test splits are released under CC BY 4.0 on the Hugging Face Hub.

Graphics.title: Skin Tokens: A Learned Compact Representation for Unified Autoregressive Rigging
Graphics.summary: The rapid proliferation of generative 3D models has created a critical bottleneck in animation pipelines: rigging. Existing automated methods are fundamentally limited by their approach to skinning, treating it as an ill-posed, high-dimensional regression task that is inefficient to optimize and is typically decoupled from skeleton generation. We posit this is a representation problem and introduce SkinTokens: a learned, compact, and discrete representation for skinning weights. By leveraging an FSQ-CVAE to capture the intrinsic sparsity of skinning, we reframe the task from continuous regression to a more tractable token sequence prediction problem. This representation enables TokenRig, a unified autoregressive framework that models the entire rig as a single sequence of skeletal parameters and SkinTokens, learning the complicated dependencies between skeletons and skin deformations. The unified model is then amenable to a reinforcement learning stage, where tailored geometric and semantic rewards improve generalization to complex, out-of-distribution assets. Quantitatively, the SkinTokens representation leads to a 98%-133% percents improvement in skinning accuracy over state-of-the-art methods, while the full TokenRig framework, refined with RL, enhances bone prediction by 17%-22%. Our work presents a unified, generative approach to rigging that yields higher fidelity and robustness, offering a scalable solution to a long-standing challenge in 3D content creation.

Graphics.title: PhysSkin++: Real-Time and Generalizable Physics-Based Animation via Self-Supervised Neural Skinning
Graphics.summary: Generalizing real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and spatial discretizations remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce PhysSkin++, a physics-informed framework that learns continuous neural skinning fields from static geometries to construct compact deformation subspaces. Specifically, we propose a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder that predicts shape-dependent deformation subspaces without per-object network training. To learn these subspaces without simulation trajectories, we develop a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning strategy that combines skinning-field normalization with conflict-aware gradient correction, stabilizing joint optimization under physical and orthogonality constraints. The learned representation supports efficient reduced dynamics with user control and contact interactions, together with direct animation binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians. For prescribed rig animation, we further introduce a self-supervised complementarity objective to learn complementary elastic responses without enforcing complementarity constraints at runtime. Experiments demonstrate cross-shape generalization of the learned skinning fields, real-time reduced simulation, and applications to controllable, collision-aware, and rig-complementary animation.

Graphics.title: Quantized High-Performance High-Order Moment-Encoded LBM
Graphics.summary: Lattice Boltzmann methods (LBM) are widely used for visually rich fluid simulation, but their high memory bandwidth and storage requirements limit GPU performance and scalability, especially when coupled with complex geometry. Recent high-order moment-encoded LBM (HOME-LBM) reduces memory cost by storing compact velocity moments and performing collision directly in moment space, but its tightly coupled boundary treatment introduces divergent control flow. We present a high-performance, quantized HOME-LBM framework for large-scale turbulent fluid-solid simulations on a single GPU. Our geometry-decoupled computation scheme separates the regular fluid update from a sparse solid-correction stage, isolating geometry-dependent computations to improve GPU efficiency. To further reduce storage and memory traffic, we develop a reduced-precision representation for HOME-LBM by combining von Neumann stability analysis, empirical moment-range estimation, and runtime decomposition of second-order moments to control quantization error. We evaluate our approach on real-time demonstrations and large-scale examples using both D3Q19 and D3Q27 lattices, with additional 2D and 3D numerical experiments assessing accuracy and stability. Across the tested benchmarks, our framework substantially accelerates the original FP32 HOME-LBM implementation, with a maximum speedup of 32.5x on the Hilbert-curve geometry. Moment storage is reduced by 50% in fluid-only simulations and 25% in fluid-solid coupling examples, while maintaining numerical stability, fidelity, and high visual quality. In the static delta-wing benchmark, our solver achieves a 5.2x speedup over Leapfrog Flow Maps (LFM) under the tested configuration.

Graphics.title: Does Tile Granularity Matter? An Empirical Study of Vector Tile Compression for Map Rendering with MapLibre Tiles
Graphics.summary: Vector tiles are delivered as pyramids of small, independently encoded units, whose spatial granularity is largely determined by the tiling scheme. We investigate how this granularity affects compression in column-oriented MapLibre Tiles (MLT), using feature-oriented Mapbox Vector Tiles (MVT) as a baseline. Five heterogeneous geospatial datasets were encoded as conventional tile pyramids and as two denser variants grouping the area of 2 x 2 or 4 x 4 conventional tiles into one encoding unit at approximately matched logical levels of detail. Compared with conventional tiling, the 4 x 4 variant increased MLT's raw size saving over MVT by 1.0-7.3 percentage points across all five datasets. After per-tile gzip, the saving increased by 1.5-6.4 points in four datasets and decreased by 1.4 points in one. Coarser granularity lengthened MLT streams and reduced structural overhead in every dataset. The largest raw gains occurred where conventional tiles had the shortest streams: as mean values per stream rose from 27 to 2,075 across datasets, the raw gain decreased from 7.3 to 1.0 points. Encoded payload bytes per value also declined, with the strongest reductions in two datasets. For the two sparse datasets, coarser units reduced bytes per vertex across both formats, with or without gzip; the resulting 4 x 4 MLT+gzip archives were 71% and 33% smaller than the conventional ones. Thus, the measured compression advantage of MLT depends on spatial encoding-unit granularity, and conventional fine-grained tiling can understate the potential of column-oriented compression.
Graphics.comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Source code and experimental data available on Zenodo

Graphics.title: FluidGen: Physics-Aware Fluid Video Generation via Motion-Guided Post-Training
Graphics.summary: Video generation models produce visually compelling motion but systematically fail on fluid phenomena, including smoke, fire, and explosion debris, where outputs lack coherent vortical structure and collapse to bland dynamics that violate the physics of real fluids. Classical solvers achieve high physical fidelity but require detailed 3D scenes and carefully tuned parameters, making them impractical for in-the-wild imagery and video generation. We address this gap by injecting a data-driven fluid prior into a pre-trained video model, trained on a mixture of high-fidelity Houdini simulation data with paired velocity-field ground truth and curated in-the-wild fluid video data for appearance diversity. The core of our approach is a dual stream architecture that predicts per-frame velocity fields alongside RGB, supervised by simulation ground truth. This auxiliary signal regularizes generation toward physically consistent motion and exposes an interpretable physical quantity that we further leverage as a reward for velocity-aware direct preference optimization. Our model produces substantially more realistic fluid dynamics sequences than strong video baselines and optimization-based methods. Project page: https://y-zheng18.github.io/FluidGen/

Graphics.title: Neural Controlled Directional Frame Generation for Sprite Animation
Graphics.summary: Sprite-based animation remains prevalent in video game development, but production workflows require capabilities beyond traditional in-betweening. While existing neural interpolation methods can generate intermediate frames, animators also need forward extrapolation to predict motion continuations and backward extrapolation for editing and reverse-engineering existing sprite sheets. Current video generation models either operate on natural video content with stochastic diffusion sampling incompatible with production requirements, or focus exclusively on interpolation without addressing extrapolation tasks. We present a deep learning approach for controlled directional frame generation in sprite animation using three specialized expert models that share identical U-Net encoder-decoder architectures and several domain-specific modifications, including RGBA-aware processing, multi-scale flow refinement, pixel-shuffle upsampling, and alpha-gated blending. Each model is trained on different temporal orderings of the same curated dataset: previous (frames 2,3>1), middle (frames 1,3>2), and next (frames 1,2>3). We demonstrate that only 280 carefully curated sprite triplets enable effective training for all three directional tasks without requiring massive generic datasets. Evaluation on 42 test triplets using the FLIP metric shows that all three models achieve comparable quality--previous (0.26), middle (0.26), and next (0.27)--with no significant degradation for extrapolation versus interpolation, outperforming general-purpose baselines by 17-57%. With deterministic single-pass generation and compact model, our method provides the first practical solution for controllable any-position frame generation specifically tailored for pixel art sprite animation workflows, validating that quality-over-quantity data curation enables specialized deep learning for niche visual domains.

Graphics.title: StippleDiffusion: Capacity-Constrained Stippling using Controlled Diffusion
Graphics.summary: Stipple patterns, point sets whose local density tracks a target image, are traditionally produced by per-density iterative optimizers, which are slow, non-differentiable, and must be re-run from scratch for each new target. Learned alternatives have so far addressed only unconditional point generation; capacity-constrained, image-conditioned stippling has remained out of reach. We present the first diffusion-based sampler that simultaneously satisfies a learned local point-distribution prior and a continuous, image-defined capacity constraint at inference. The method is a ControlNet branch built on top of an optimal-transport-grid point-set diffusion baseline, conditioned on the target density map and a high-resolution image. Two design choices make the combination tractable: training and inference are restricted to the late-stage denoising regime, initialized from a density-weighted rejection sample, and the standard zero-convolution injection is replaced with a sigmoid-gated 1x1 projection that preserves the base model's blue-noise structure under hard density signals. A single trained checkpoint accepts arbitrary target densities at inference, generalizes to point budgets that were not seen during training, and produces stipples in time nearly independent of the output point count. On the Icons-50 benchmark, our learned sampler reaches parity with per-density-optimized baselines on every reported metric while remaining differentiable end-to-end.

Graphics.title: Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
Graphics.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting grows a dense scene from a sparse initialization through adaptive density control (ADC), driven by per-Gaussian statistics gathered during rendering. These statistics pass a frustum-based visibility filter blind to occlusion: fully occluded Gaussians still count as observed, diluting the averaged gradient signal and suppressing densification precisely where geometry is occluded. We correct this with an occlusion-aware filter that restricts densification statistics to views in which a Gaussian actually contributes, and replace the criterion's raw view-count normalizer with an average-contribution one. Integrated into a StopThePop-based framework, the two together improve every image-quality metric over the occlusion-blind baseline on occlusion-heavy scenes (up to 6% lower LPIPS), at less than half the Gaussians a view-count normalizer requires. Under the longer schedules these large scenes require, the count stays bounded where most criteria diverge, and on smaller benchmarks our method stays competitive at a fraction of the competitors' count.
Graphics.comment: Accepted at ACCV 2026 (Oral). Includes the supplementary material as appendix. Code: https://github.com/MarcelRogge/occlusion-aware-3dgs

Operating Systems.title: AgentLens: Framework-Aware Characterization and Resource Control for Heterogeneous LLM Agents
Operating Systems.summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed on shared hosts, yet their host-side resource demands remain poorly understood, limiting effective resource coordination. We present AgentLens, which combines a cross-framework workload characterization with a framework-aware resource controller for co-located agents. Across 10 frameworks and 11 matched coding tasks, we find that framework orchestration strongly shapes resource demand: framework identity explains 52.95% of peak RSS variance, compared with 4.22% for task identity, while execve events per tool call differ by 39x between MetaGPT and CAMEL. Resource dimensions are not interchangeable: peak RSS and subprocess count have a Spearman correlation of 0.13. Static budgets and framework-agnostic policies miss these structural differences and the alternation between API waiting and tool execution. AgentLens combines offline framework fingerprints with online execution-phase signals to coordinate memory through cgroup v2, without modifying framework internals. In trace-driven replay across three co-location pairs at a memory budget of 90% of aggregate peak demand, AgentLens keeps the protected worker's P95 allocation latency at 5.7-7.1 ms, improving on static allocation by 2.1-2.6x.

Operating Systems.title: gKSM: GPU Memory Deduplication at Driver Layer for Serverless LLM Inference
Operating Systems.summary:
In serverless LLM inference, cloud providers commonly locate multiple instances on a single GPU to improve utilization. However, each instance independently maintains its model weights and runtime state, making duplicate GPU memory the primary bottleneck. Memory deduplication is a widely-used technique for eliminating duplicate data in CPU systems, but extending it to GPU memory faces fundamental challenges. Effective GPU memory deduplication must avoid redundant data movement between CPU and GPU while preserving write isolation for shared pages without native copy-on-write (COW) support.
  This paper presents gKSM, a transparent GPU memory deduplication framework for serverless LLM inference. gKSM addresses these challenges through CPU-GPU collaborative hash management that offloads hash computation to GPU kernels, zero-copy model weight deduplication that eliminates duplication before model weight transfer, and a cross-privilege page fault handler that combines a lightweight kernel hook and CUDA Virtual Memory Management (VMM) remapping in the user space. gKSM also designs a stable page scanning algorithm and a reuse-aware placement policy in cluster scale. Experiments show that gKSM reduces GPU memory usage by 59.8% while maintaining high throughput compared to ServerlessLLM. Under memory constrained workloads, gKSM improves aggregate throughput by 2.15X and supports five instances concurrently. In cluster level simulation, gKSM achieves a service rate of 99.97%, compared to 78.2% for SLInfer and 26.9% for ServerlessLLM.

Operating Systems.title: InfraBench: Evaluating Infrastructure Agents Across Layers, Lifecycle, and Risk
Operating Systems.summary: Managing modern computing infrastructure has become a steadily harder problem due to the ever-increasing complexity. Recent advances in AI agents create a timely opportunity to automate infrastructure management tasks, but it remains unclear how well such agents can handle real-world infrastructure complexity. We present InfraBench, a benchmark for infrastructure agents organized around system layers, the operational lifecycle, and risk. The current prototype couples container, VM, and bare-metal backends with task-specific verifiers that distinguish functional repair from durability and cleanup, and analyzes retained action-trace findings for unsafe shortcuts. We evaluate 18 agent-model configurations on 12 seed tasks, with three attempts per task. Mean effective scores range from 45.5% to 89.2%; the strongest configuration completes 77.8% of attempts perfectly. In the available lifecycle checks, pass rates fall from 91.5% for functional repair to 80.9% for durability and 38.9% for cleanup. These results show why immediate recovery is an incomplete measure of operational capability. We use this evidence to motivate a planned expansion toward 40-60 tasks centered on managed cloud infrastructure and redesign after incidents, including provider-native Kubernetes networking. This extension is a research direction; the reported results remain those of the 12-task prototype. InfraBench, its tasks, evaluation harness, and live leaderboard are available at infraben.ch.
Operating Systems.comment: 15 pages, 6 figures. Updated evaluation with 18 agent-model configurations

Operating Systems.title: Visual Cache Reuse for Efficient Multimodal Inference
Operating Systems.summary:
Vision-language model (VLM) inference incurs substantial prefill latency and memory overhead due to the long visual token sequences of large visual inputs. Existing serving systems typically exploit exact cache reuse through prefix caching or position-independent caching, overlooking the potential of approximate caching in real-world workloads. However, directly reusing an approximate cache entry may introduce spurious visual information, which naive approaches that select a subset of important visual tokens for recomputation fail to adequately mitigate this risk.
  We present VisMemo, an efficient serving system that enables approximate KV cache reuse for modern VLMs. Its core is a system-algorithm co-design that combines an entropy-aware KV cache reuse algorithm with differentiated cache management. Specifically, VisMemo uses patch entropy to identify reuse candidates and warmup attention to prioritize recomputation based on the current query. To support the large cache capacity across GPU memory, CPU memory, and SSD storage, VisMemo applies distinct I/O and cache policies to exact and approximate hits: sparse patch-level I/O for approximate hits, prioritized retention for exact hits, and a reserved CPU victim cache for preset entries selected using offline workload priors and online reuse observations. VisMemo further optimizes the memory access path between the inference engine and the storage backend, eliminating redundant caching and unnecessary data movement. Experiments on multiple public datasets show that VisMemo preserves output quality under approximate reuse. On a real-world production trace, VisMemo increases the overall cache hit rate from 27.78% to 61.45% and reduces prefill latency by up to 48.3% at 8K input tokens.

Hardware Architecture.title: Fine-Grained Parallel Graph Algorithms Can Be Both Fast and Scalable
Hardware Architecture.summary: Making graph algorithms fast and scalable on traditional architectures and GPUs often involves breaking them into large, coarse-grained computational blocks that access similar regions of memory. We show that graph algorithms, which have tremendous vertex- and edge-level parallelism, can be scaled as fine-grained programs on suitable architectures. Specifically, we investigate graph algorithms on the UpDown architecture and show how this many-threaded, cache-less architecture enables simple, fine-grained parallel graph algorithms to be both fast and scalable. Single-node UpDown performance is 28x (geomean) over an H200 GPU, and that same program scales to 1000's of nodes. We evaluate the system three ways: simulation, analytical projection models, and selected validation studies at scale (simulation of 16,384 UpDown nodes, using 256 supercomputer nodes). These results show the UpDown system can achieve 680K giga-traversed edges per second (GTEPS) for PageRank and 989K GTEPS BFS, exceeding prior results significantly.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 13 pages, 12 figures, 7 tables

Hardware Architecture.title: Heuristic-Driven Resource Optimization for Decoupled Memory Channels on FPGAs
Hardware Architecture.summary: Determining OpenCL channel depths for Decoupled Access-Execute (DAE) architectures in High-Level Synthesis (HLS) is critical for balancing performance and hardware efficiency. Conventional static analysis tools often over-provision these memory channels to ensure performance safety, leading to significant resource stranding. This paper presents an expansion of an LLVM-based static analysis framework, originally proposed for automated DAE generation, by introducing a hardware-aware refinement layer. We identify a counter-intuitive Performance Inversion Paradox linked to baseline memory stalls, where high-stall, grid-based kernels reach peak performance at minimal channel depths and suffer up to a 61% throughput degradation when depths are increased. We propose a Heuristic Refinement Layer that optimizes OpenCL channel depths based on this correlation between baseline stalls and performance saturation. Experimental results demonstrate that our expanded framework successfully identifies the Minimal Peak Performance point across various benchmarks. By avoiding the performance traps of standard over-provisioning, we achieve a 2.52x improvement in Resource Efficiency for an illustrative HotSpot application. This approach maintains peak execution speedup while ensuring the leanest possible hardware profile, outperforming conservative tool-based static predictions.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 6 pages. Accepted version of a paper published in the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Interdisciplinary Approaches in Technology and Management for Social Innovation (IATMSI)

Hardware Architecture.title: Cryogenic Recharacterization of a Commercial 22 nm FD-SOI Foundry Standard-Cell Library
Hardware Architecture.summary: Wiring and bandwidth bottlenecks between a quantum processor and room-temperature electronics can be reduced by placing digital control at the cryogenic stage, but commercial foundry standard-cell libraries are not specified for operation at 4 K. A cryogenic recharacterization flow is therefore developed for a commercial 22 nm FD-SOI foundry standard-cell library using commercially available cryogenic compact-device models, while retaining the original cell circuits, layouts, logic functions, and implementation semantics and remaining compatible with the commercial synthesis, place-and-route, and signoff methodology used at room temperature. Body-bias dependence is quantified over 38,640 matched slew/load points at zero, +/-0.9 V, and +/-1.8 V body bias. Relative to full bias, zero-bias operation increases the median rising and falling delays by 38.6x and 33.0x, while approximately 90% of transitions exceed the foundry-defined maximum-transition envelope. The 0.8 V-to-0.4 V level shifter is even more sensitive to body bias: its worst-case falling delay decreases from 30.6 ns at zero bias to 0.56 ns at +/-1.8 V. For the outbound 0.4 V-to-0.8 V crossing, driving the 0.8 V receiver without a level shifter dissipates 57.7 uW of static power per bit at full bias, against 0.196 nW when level-shifted. In post-route analysis of the unchanged extracted physical database of a fabricated 32-bit ALU, the register-to-register setup boundary increases from 1.3 MHz at zero bias to 37.9 MHz at +/-0.9 V and 132.9 MHz at +/-1.8 V.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems (ISCAS 2027)

Hardware Architecture.title: PAGE404: Breaking GPU Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
Hardware Architecture.summary: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. By eliminating the conventional PCIe bottleneck for CPU-GPU data movement, this design establishes a unified memory domain that scales to the capacities demanded by generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The architecture also introduces hardware-assisted page migration: driven by access counters, the system dynamically promotes frequently accessed pages from host CPU memory to GPU DRAM to improve memory locality. We study the security of this emerging architecture against new side- and covert-channel attacks targeting its page migration support. We analyze counter-driven migration across both the hardware mechanisms and the UVM driver's interrupt-handling pipeline, and identify two side-channel vulnerabilities: one rooted in the shared structure of access counters, and the other in the driver's response to migration interrupts. We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.

Programming Languages.title: A Trust Ledger and an Execution Check for CPG-Based C-to-Lean 4 Autoformalization: Separating Declined from Silently Incorrect Translations
Programming Languages.summary: Verifying large C codebases requires translating them into formally checkable semantics, but most autoformalization work reports a single aggregate success rate that conflates two different failure modes: code the translator declined to handle and code the translator translated incorrectly. We present a deterministic code-property-graph (CPG)-based exporter that translates C source into a small Lean~4 core semantics under a three-tier correctness discipline: hole-free, call-closed, and dynamic-hole-risk, that keeps these modes distinct. Applied to a re-export of the SQLite source tree (8{,}602 functions, over 1.5~million AST nodes), the exporter translates 5{,}222 functions (60.7\%) hole-free, of which only 2{,}134 (24.8\%) are call-closed, a $2.4\times$ gap a single rate would hide. Both figures are reported in a full per-construct trust ledger rather than a single score. Our main contribution is methodological: a protocol for separating constructs that are fundamentally unresolvable by whole-program static analysis (such as public API boundaries) from constructs that only look that way. For example, we retracted our own ``impossible'' classification of function-pointer/vtable dispatch after tracing a concrete counterexample in the target codebase.
