This property was first introduced by Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya (SODA 2018), who used it to show a lower bound on testing the $\texttt{Dyck}$ languages, where $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ is the language consisting of balanced sequences of parentheses over $m$ parenthesis types. They showed that testing $\texttt{ResStringEq}$ on inputs of length $n$ requires $Ω(n^{1/5})$ queries, and presented a reduction from testing $\texttt{ResStringEq}$ to testing $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ for any $m \geq 2$. Furthermore, they showed that $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ can be tested with $O(n^{2/5+δ})$ queries for every constant proximity parameter, where $δ>0$ is an arbitrarily small constant.
  In this work, we nearly close the gap, by showing that testing $\texttt{ResStringEq}$, and hence $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ (for any $m\geq 2$), requires $Ω(n^{2/5})$ queries. We also show a stronger lower bound of $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ for testers that make non-adaptive queries. We establish that the $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ bound is nearly tight, by presenting a non-adaptive tester for $\texttt{ResStringEq}$ that uses $O(n^{1/2+δ})$ queries for an arbitrarily small constant $δ>0$. Furthermore, we extend this non-adaptive tester to the $\texttt{Dyck}$ languages, with the same query complexity. Finally, we improve the dependence on the proximity parameter $ε$ in the tester of Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya, reducing it from $O(1/ε)^{\mathrm{poly}(1/δ)}$ to $O(1/ε)^{O(\log(1/δ))}$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Output-linear time enumeration of potential maximal cliques
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
First defined by Bouchitté and Todinca, Potential Maximal Cliques (PMC) are a well studied notion in graph theory due to its numerous applications. The PMCs of an undirected graph $G$ are defined as the maximal cliques of the minimal triangulations of $G$. Their number can be exponential in the size of the graph. PMCs were crucial in the design of a polynomial-time algorithm which solves Maximum Weight Independent Set on $P_6$-free graphs (Grzesik, Klimošová, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, 2020). They also play a central role in the proposal of a polynomial-time algorithm to solve Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ (Fomin, Todinca, Villanger, 2013).
  Last but not least, certainly one of the main application of PMCs is the existence of an exact dynamic-programming algorithm to determine the treewidth of a graph (Fomin, Kratsch, Todinca, Villanger, 2008) which uses its list of PMCs as an input. In fact, the enumeration of PMCs stands as the bottleneck for the computation of treewidth with this method: the PMC-enumeration step takes output-quadratic time (Bouchitté, Todinca, 2002) while the dynamic-programming one takes a time linear in the number of PMCs. This two-step procedure was proven to be among the most performing approaches in practice to determine treewidth.
  Answering a longstanding open question, we propose an algorithm to enumerate PMCs in output-linear time, i.e. a running time linear in the number of PMCs. This offers nice perspectives not only from the theoretical viewpoint - better running time for the PMC-based methods determining treewidth, for Minimum Fill-In and Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ - but also from the practical side, with the possibility to propose top-performance implementation.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: This paper was accepted at SODA 2027. 54 pages, 18 figures

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: ARRIVAL in cube-root subexponential time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the ARRIVAL problem, a token travels through a switch digraph: at every vertex, it leaves along one of two out-arcs, and the two are used alternately. The question is which of two terminals the token reaches first. ARRIVAL lies in $\mathsf{NP} \cap \mathsf{coNP}$, but no polynomial-time algorithm is known.The fastest known algorithms turn some vertices into terminals and search for consistent guesses of the numbers of tokens that these vertices send out. The first, due to Gärtner et al. [ICALP 2021], searches all vertices at once with an algorithm for fixed points of monotone maps, and the second, due to Haslebacher [ICALP 2025], searches one vertex at a time by binary search. Both search for a fixed point of the same map, which returns how many tokens arrive at the guessed vertices.
  We guess the vertices in blocks of $k$, between these two extremes, which needs a search in $k$ dimensions with few evaluations of this map. To do so, we build on the connection between ARRIVAL and $\ell_1$-contractions established in the second of these works. We search with $\ell_1$-centerpoints of the remaining guesses, which are guaranteed to exist by Haslebacher et al. [FOCS 2025], and which we approximate deterministically. In order to prove our results, we show how to find the least fixed points of maps from $\{0, \ldots, N\}^k$ to itself that have unit increments.
  For ARRIVAL on $n$-vertex switch digraphs, this gives run time $2^{\mathcal{O}(n^{1/3} \cdot \log^{2/3} n)}$, improving the previous time bound of $n^{\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})}$. We work with the more general \garrival problem, with many tokens and several terminals, and solve it in the same time when there are at most $2^n$ tokens.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Subjective Valuations Make It Hard to be Fair: The Complexity of Resource Allocation to Groups of Agents
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the parameterized complexity of finding an EF1 allocation of indivisible items in the group-sharing setting, which has received increasing attention in recent years. There, items are not allocated to individual agents but rather to one of two (or possibly more) groups, and agents within that group all share the assigned items. We consider both the "fixed" (EF1-Fix) and "variable" (EF1-Var) group cases, where in the former the assignments of agents to groups are prescribed. While both are NP-hard in the classical sense, we show that their algorithmic behavior differs significantly from the parameterized perspective. As our main results, we:
  (1) prove that both cases are NP-hard even when the number of agents is a small constant;
  (2) circumvent this hardness by establishing fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Var w.r.t. the number of "subjective" items, that is, items which are viewed as chores or goods by different agents---but rule out an analogous result for EF1-Fix; and
  (3) establish fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Fix w.r.t. the number of item types, but link the existence of an analogous fixed-parameter algorithm for EF1-Var to a fundamental open question in the setting of Integer Linear Programming.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Practical and Space-Efficient LZ77 and LZ Pre-Compression via String Synchronizing Sets
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Lempel-Ziv (LZ77) factorization decomposes a text into the least possible number $z$ of phrases that each refer to an earlier occurrence. It is this phrase count, rather than the encoded size, that governs the size of LZ-based compressed indexes, and computing a factorization with few phrases is a time and space bottleneck in their construction. In practice, computing LZ77 quickly typically requires the suffix array. In theory, the exact LZ77 factorization, and a 3-approximation of it, can be computed more space-efficiently without the full suffix array [SPIRE 2023]. These algorithms have remained unimplemented, because two of their components resist a direct implementation: a lookup table that degenerates to patterns of length at most two for realistic inputs, and an orthogonal range reporting data structure that is impractical. We replace both, fine-tune every remaining stage, and obtain the first practical implementation, which runs in space close to the text rather than to the suffix array. On one thread, our 3-approximation factorizes 12-19x faster than the classical LPF algorithm while using 14x less memory; on 32 threads, even our exact algorithm is 1.4-2.9x faster than parallel LPF, at 9x less memory. In practice the approximation ratio stays far below 3. As a side result, passing only the perfect phrases of our 3-approximation to a downstream compressor yields a precompressor that is on par with the state of the art [Dinklage, SEA 2026] in compression ratio, and better in memory consumption and parallel throughput.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Full version of the ALENEX 2027 paper

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Assortment optimization given basket shopping behavior using the Ising model
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In markets where customers tend to purchase baskets of products rather than single products, assortment optimization is a major challenge for retailers. Removing a product from a retailer's assortment can result in a severe drop in aggregate demand if this product is a complement to other products. Therefore, accounting for the complementarity effect is essential when making assortment decisions. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework designed to address this problem. We model customers' choices using the binary Ising model, which is a special case of a Markov random field. This model captures pairwise demand dependencies as well as the individual attractiveness of each product, with binary variables indicating whether products are included in the purchased basket. For estimation, we utilize existing methods developed for the spin formulation of the Ising model and then apply a parameter transformation to express the fitted model in the binary form used for assortment optimization. We show that the assortment optimization problem under the Ising model is NP-hard. We also provide multiple theoretical insights into the structure of the optimal assortments based on the graphical representation of the Ising model, and propose several heuristic algorithms that can be used to obtain high-quality solutions to the assortment optimization problem. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the developed simulated annealing procedure leads to an expected profit gain of 15% compared to offering an unoptimized assortment (where all products are included) and around 5% compared to using a revenue-ordered heuristic algorithm.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Splitting Planar Necklaces with Few Straight Cuts
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In the classical necklace splitting problem, beads of different colors lie on a line, and the goal is to divide them among $k$ agents using as few cuts as possible so that every agent receives the same number of beads of each color. We study the planar analog in which a cut is a full straight line and the objective is minimizing the number of lines: $m$ points colored red and blue must be separated by straight-line cuts into regions that can be allocated to $k$ agents so that each agent receives the same number of points of each color. Projection to a line gives $2(k-1)$ cuts, and $k-1$ are sometimes necessary; we give algorithms, static and dynamic, that provably close part of this gap. We develop several approaches that capitalize on the extra degree of freedom: a ``star'' search that produces solutions with as few as $\lceil \frac{k}{2} \rceil$ cuts and never more than $k$ whenever a fair contiguous circular partition exists, with further guarantees for evenly spaced input, and a general algorithm that produces at most $k + \log_2(k+1) - 2$ cuts in $Θ(m \log k)$ time, built on a one-dimensional necklace splitting subroutine that requires no presorting. We then adapt the general algorithm to a dynamic setting, maintaining exact fairness and the cut bound under arbitrary relocation of points, with expected update time that scales with the total distance moved.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Results for the Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set Problem
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the \emph{Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set} problem (MEG-Set), which asks for a minimum-cardinality set $M$ of vertices of an undirected graph $G$ of $n$ vertices such that every edge of $G$ belongs to all shortest paths between some pair of vertices in $M$.
  We present new approximation and hardness results for MEG-Set. On the positive side, we design a deterministic polynomial-time $O(n^{1/3}\log^{2/3}n)$-approximation algorithm, improving upon the previously best-known $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ approximation ratio. On the negative side, for every constant $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we prove that the problem admits no polynomial-time $\big(2^{\log^{1-\varepsilon} n}\big)$-approximation algorithm, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq \mathsf{DTIME}(n^{\operatorname{polylog} n})$. This substantially improves upon the previously known logarithmic inapproximability bound. We also prove that \megset is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard on planar $2$-degenerate graphs, whereas $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness was previously known for $1$-apex $2$-degenerate graphs.
  We conclude by observing a connection between monitoring edge-geodetic sets and subsetwise distance preservers, i.e., subgraphs that preserve distances between all pairs of vertices in $S\subseteq V(G)$. Specifically, we show that any upper bound on the size of the latter yields a lower bound on the size of the former.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Online Load Balancing in the Two-Norm
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the online load balancing problem on unrelated machines, with the objective of minimizing the square of the $\ell_2$ norm of the loads on the machines. The greedy algorithm of Awerbuch et al. (STOC'95) is optimal for deterministic algorithms and achieves a competitive ratio of $3 + 2 \sqrt{2} \approx 5.828$, and an improved $5$-competitive randomized algorithm based on independent rounding has been shown by Caragiannis (SODA'08). In this work, we present the first algorithm breaking the barrier of $5$ on the competitive ratio, achieving a bound of $5-c$ for some $c \geq 0.0157$. To obtain this result, we use a new primal-dual framework to analyze this problem based on a natural semidefinite programming relaxation, together with an online implementation of a correlated randomized rounding procedure of Im and Shadloo (SODA'20). This novel primal-dual framework also yields new, simple and unified proofs of the competitive ratio of the $(3 + 2 \sqrt{2})$-competitive greedy algorithm, the $5$-competitive randomized independent rounding algorithm, and that of a new $4$-competitive optimal fractional algorithm. We also provide lower bounds showing that the previous best randomized algorithm is optimal among independent rounding algorithms, that our new fractional algorithm is optimal, and that a simple greedy algorithm is optimal for the closely related online scheduling problem $R || \sum w_j C_j$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An Exact Polynomial-Time Algorithm for the Minimum Shared-Power Edge Cut Problem
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Minimum Shared-Power Edge Cut (MSPEC) problem seeks to disconnect two designated terminals with minimum total power by assigning powers to graph vertices and deleting every edge for which the sum of the powers at its endpoints reaches its edge weight. Previous work gave a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for this problem, while its exact computational complexity remained open. We prove that general MSPEC with nonnegative edge weights can be solved exactly in polynomial time. Specifically, we first use linear programming duality for each fixed cut to reformulate MSPEC as minimizing the maximum terminal-relaxed matching weight over all $s$-$t$ cuts. Then, we construct a terminal-copy extended graph that transforms the maximum-weight matching model with unconstrained terminal capacities for a fixed cut into an equivalent ordinary maximum-weight matching model. Next, we extend the submodularity of the unweighted maximum-matching cut function to nonnegative edge weights and prove that the restriction obtained by fixing the terminal copies on prescribed sides remains submodular. Consequently, MSPEC reduces to exact submodular function minimization. Once an optimal cut is obtained, a corresponding optimal power assignment can be recovered. This result resolves the open question concerning the exact computational complexity of general MSPEC.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A 2/3-Approximation Algorithm for the Residual Maximum Matching Problem in General Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The residual maximum matching problem asks for a maximum matching whose deletion leaves a graph with the largest possible matching number. For unweighted graphs, previous work provides a $1/2$-approximation guarantee in general graphs and a $2/3$ guarantee in graphs with a perfect matching. We present a $2/3$-approximation algorithm running in $O(n^5)$ time, extending the latter guarantee to general graphs. The algorithm improves the residual matching number through single-edge exchanges involving free vertices. We prove that, for any maximum matching that admits no further improvement by such exchanges, the residual matching number is at least $2/3$ of the optimum, and we give an example showing that this bound is tight.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An Analytic 0.48-Approximation for Non-Monotone k-Submodular Maximization under a Matroid Constraint
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a randomized polynomial-time $0.48$-approximation for maximizing a nonnegative non-monotone $k$-submodular function under a matroid constraint, for every $k\ge2$. The algorithm combines a top-two label rule with a nested-chain potential and maximum-weight matroid bases. Its analysis reduces the approximation guarantee to a one-dimensional time allocation: a uniform local lower bound leads to a linear differential equation, concavity closes the remaining interval, and two elementary budgets complete the proof. A strict saving in the time budget absorbs sampling and discretization errors, yielding the exact $0.48$ guarantee in the value-oracle model.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 22 pages, 1 figure, 1 table; author list updated to include Wenguo Yang

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: FPTAS for Polygonal Multi-Robot Motion Planning
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study multi-robot motion planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots. The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain $\mathcal{W}$ with $n$ vertices and $k$ robots $R_1,\dots,R_k$ translating in $\mathcal{W}$ each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity. Given a source configuration $\mathbf{s}$ and a target configuration $\mathbf{t}$ of the robots in $\mathcal{W}$, the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ that is shortest with respect to some cost function. We present the first fully polynomial-time approximation schemes (FPTAS) for motion planning with any fixed number $k$ of robots, under the min-sum objective, the min-max objective, and the min-makespan objective. Here, the min-sum variant aims to minimize the total traveling distance of all robots, the min-max variant aims to minimize the maximum traveling distance of a single robot, and the min-makespan variant aims to minimize the total time cost under the assumption that all robots move with a maximum speed $1$. The algorithm directly generalizes to the problem in any fixed dimension $d$, with a polytope environment and polytope robots. Our result settles an open question of Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, Steiger [SODA'24] and Agarwal, Holmgren, Steiger [SODA'26], who gave an FPTAS for $k=2$ unit-square robots and a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for a fixed number $k$ of unit-square or unit-disk robots, respectively. Compared to the previous results, our algorithm is substantially simpler.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Algorithms for Computing Longest Unbordered Factors on Run-Length Encoded Strings
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A border of a string is a non-empty proper prefix of the string that is also a suffix. A string is called unbordered if it has no border. The longest unbordered factor is a fundamental notion in stringology, closely related to string periodicity. This paper addresses the longest unbordered factor problem: given a string of length $n$, the goal is to compute its longest factor that is unbordered. While recent work has achieved subquadratic and near-linear time algorithms for this problem, the best known worst-case time complexity remains $O(n \log n)$ [Kociumaka et al., ISAAC 2018]. In this paper, we investigate the problem in the context of compressed string processing, focusing specifically on run-length encoded (RLE) strings. We first present a simple yet crucial structural observation relating unbordered factors and RLE-compressed strings. Building on this, we propose an algorithm that solves the problem in $O(m^{1.5} \log^2 m)$ time and $O(m \log^2 m)$ space, where $m$ is the size of the RLE-compressed input string. Furthermore, we propose another algorithm for the problem that runs in average $O(m \log^2 m)$ time and $O(m\log m)$ space: The average-case bound holds under an exponent-bounded random-input model, in which the input is chosen uniformly from the strings of RLE size $m$ whose run exponents are at most a given bound $E\geq 2$. Our approaches extend key ideas from [Gawrychowski et al., SPIRE 2015] to the RLE setting through new combinatorial insights. When the RLE size $m$ is sufficiently small compared to $n$, our algorithms achieve linear-time behavior in $n$, potentially leading to improved performance over existing methods in such cases.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Accepted for Theory of Computing Systems

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: ${\varepsilon}$-Cost Sharding: Scaling Hypergraph-Based Data Structures to Trillions of Keys
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We describe a simple and yet very scalable implementation of static functions (VFunc) and of static filters (VFilter) based on hypergraphs. We introduce the idea of $\varepsilon$-cost sharding, which allows us to build structures that can manage trillions of keys, at the same time increasing memory locality in hypergraph-based constructions. Contrarily to the commonly used HEM sharding method, $\varepsilon$-cost sharding does not require to store of additional information, and does not introduce dependencies in the computation chain; its only cost is that of few arithmetical instructions, and of a relative increase $\varepsilon$ in space usage. We apply $\varepsilon$-cost sharding to the classical MWHC construction, but we obtain the best result by combining Dietzfelbinger and Walzer's fuse graphs for large shards with lazy Gaussian elimination for small shards. We obtain large structures with an overhead of 10.5% with respect to the information-theoretical lower bound and with a query time that is a few nanoseconds away from the query time of the non-sharded version, which is the fastest currently available within the same space bounds. Besides comparing our structures with a non-sharded version, we contrast its tradeoffs with bumped ribbon constructions, a space-saving alternative to hypergraph-based static functions and filters, which provide optimum space consumption but slow construction and query time (though construction can be parallelized very efficiently). We build offline a trillion-key filter using commodity hardware in just 60 ns/key. Finally, we show that $\varepsilon$-cost sharding and fuse graphs carry over with no effort to data structures that reduce to static functions, such as monotone minimal perfect hash functions and compressed static functions.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved rapid phase ordering for Ising dynamics on random regular graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study Glauber dynamics for the Ising model on random $d$-regular graphs with $n$ vertices at low temperature, in the regime $β\geq C/d$ where $C,d$ are sufficiently large constants. In this regime, the full mixing time is exponential in $n$, because of the bottleneck between the two dominant phases: configurations with a majority of plus spins and configurations with a majority of minus spins. We show that, for sufficiently large $d$, if the dynamics is initialized with an excess of at least $ε_{C,d} n$ plus spins over minus spins, then it quasi-equilibrates in time $O(\log n)$ to the Gibbs measure conditioned on positive magnetization. In addition, the required bias $ε_{C,d}$ can be chosen so that $ε_{C,d}\to 0$ as $d,C\to\infty$.
  Previous bound of \cite{GSS25+} in the Ising and large-$d$ setting required $β\gtrsim (\log d)/d$. A key difficulty is that, even from the all-plus initialization, one must control the propagation of negative information in spacetime in a low-temperature model with strong local correlations. We address this by developing a new bootstrap approach to proving subcriticality of disagreement clusters under the grand coupling.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Cascade: GPU-Accelerated Out-of-Core Suffix Array Construction for LLM Corpora
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Suffix arrays power deduplication, contamination testing, and training data attribution over the corpora used to train large language models, and must be rebuilt for every new corpus or tokenizer. However, constructing them at scale is slow. infini-gram's indexing pipeline takes about two days to process 1.4 trillion tokens on its authors' 128-core CPU server. GPU-accelerated constructors are an order of magnitude faster, but their working sets must fit in GPU memory. Partitioning the corpus only moves this limit to host memory. Sorting the suffixes of one partition needs the ranks of suffixes in other partitions, which existing designs keep in a corpus-wide rank table that must stay in memory.
  We present Cascade, a GPU-accelerated out-of-core suffix-array constructor. Its partitions each own a fixed, contiguous range of the final suffix array, so the GPU sorts them independently and never merges them. Cascade then replaces the rank table with streamed rank exchange. Ranks are sent directly to the partitions that need them, and an invariant makes partition-local ranks sufficient for every comparison. With no rank table, intermediate data spills across GPU memory, host memory, and SSD as the corpus grows, and host memory only needs to hold the text.
  On seven corpora of 8-238 billion tokens, Cascade builds suffix arrays on a single GPU server 3.0-8.2x faster end to end than infini-gram's pipeline, and its construction is 6.3-11.4x faster than libsais's. It indexes the 198-billion-token C4 corpus and the 238-billion-token Pile in 23 and 37 minutes end to end, both of which exceed libsais's host-memory capacity on the same server. A batched query engine over the index reproduces infini-gram's counts at median speedups of 10.8-32.6x, with the index in GPU memory, host memory, or on SSD.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Shaving Logs via Large Sieve Inequality: Faster Algorithms for Sparse Convolution and More
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In sparse convolution-type problems, a common technique is to hash the input integers modulo a random prime $p\in [Q/2,Q]$ for some parameter $Q$, which reduces the range of the input integers while preserving their additive structure. However, this hash family suffers from two drawbacks, which led to bottlenecks in many state-of-the-art algorithms: (1) The collision probability of two elements from $[N]$ is $O(\frac{\log N}{Q})$ rather than $O(\frac{1}{Q})$; (2) It is difficult to derandomize the choice of $p$; known derandomization techniques lead to super-logarithmic overhead [Chan, Lewenstein STOC'15].
  In this paper, we partially overcome these drawbacks in certain scenarios, via novel applications of the large sieve inequality from analytic number theory. Consequently, we obtain the following improved algorithms for various problems (in the standard word RAM model):
  Sparse Nonnegative Convolution: We obtain an $O(t\log t)$-time Las Vegas algorithm that computes the convolution $A\star B$ of two nonnegative integer vectors $A,B$, where $t$ is the output sparsity $\|A\star B\|_0$. Moreover, our algorithm terminates in $O(t\log t)$ time with $1-1/\mathrm{poly}(t)$ probability.
  Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances: Given a length-$m$ pattern $P$ and a length-$n$ text $T$, we obtain a deterministic $O(n\sqrt{m\log \log m})$-time algorithm that exactly computes the Hamming distance between $P$ and every length-$m$ substring of $T$.
  Sparse General Convolution: We also give a Monte Carlo $O(t\log t)$ time algorithm for sparse convolution with possibly negative input in the restricted case where the length $N$ of the input vectors satisfies $N\le t^{1.99}$.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: v1: appeared at STOC 2024. v2: accepted to SICOMP after major revision

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Nonlinear Exchange Dynamics for Independent Sets
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In recent years, nonlinear dynamics derived from kinetic theory have gained attention in the context of sampling configurations of spin systems such as the Ising model. We focus on nonlinear dynamics for the hard-core model, a canonical spin system with hard constraints that specifies a distribution over independent sets in a graph, weighted by their sizes. We explore two distinct types of nonlinear dynamics: the mean-field dynamics, which preserves the density (or average size) of independent sets, and the single-site dynamics, which preserves the marginal vector (i.e., the occupancy probabilities of the vertices). These dynamics are natural stochastic processes for sampling from the hard-core model with a specified density or marginal vector, respectively, both of which are canonical instances of maximum entropy distributions that have been studied in various contexts.
  In contrast to linear Markov chains, there is a significant lack of a fundamental theoretical framework for nonlinear dynamics. We develop foundational theoretical tools for analyzing nonlinear dynamics within the context of the hard-core model. We establish almost linear convergence of both the mean-field and single-site dynamics at sufficiently low density through novel coupling arguments. We also establish exponential decay of relative entropy for the mean-field dynamics all the way up to the critical density. Additionally, we design new algorithms for sampling from the hard-core distribution with either a specified density or a specified marginal vector. These algorithms are based on a related linear Markov chain, called the particle-system dynamics and inspired by the so-called Kac's program, that approximates the associated nonlinear dynamics. As we demonstrate in the paper, they are comparable in time complexity, but simpler to implement, than traditional approaches based on learning parameter values.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Truthful Calibration Measures for Sequential Prediction
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Calibration requires probabilistic reports to be conditionally unbiased and reliably interpretable as probabilities. A calibration measure assigns numerical error to miscalibrated reports. Haghtalab et al. (2024) proposed an approximately truthful calibration measure for online prediction, leaving open whether exact truthfulness is compatible with completeness and soundness. We resolve this question negatively for sequential binary prediction: exact truthfulness is incompatible with completeness and soundness, even for independent outcomes. We then show that this impossibility is specific to exact truthfulness. On the positive side, we give two general reductions that transform a base calibration measure satisfying a uniform completeness condition into additively and multiplicatively approximately truthful measures, respectively. Applying the multiplicative reduction, for every $0<\varepsilon<1$ we construct a sound and complete calibration measure that is $1+\exp\left(-Ω(T^{1-\varepsilon})\right)$-multiplicatively truthful. This improves the approximate truthfulness guarantee of Haghtalab et al. (2024). We also prove a general transfer theorem showing that the uniform completeness of one calibration measure transfers to another when they are quantitatively related. Using this result, we show that every consistent calibration measure (Blasiok et al., 2023) satisfies uniform completeness and can serve as the base calibration measure to achieve $1 + o(1)$ multiplicative truthfulness.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A 55-Addition Rank-23 Scheme for $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication via Exact Two-Sided Minimization
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a scheme that multiplies two $3\times3$ matrices with 23 multiplications and 55 additions over any ring, one addition below the previous record of 56 (Sun, 2026) and the first below 56 for exact non-commutative $3\times3$ multiplication without a change of basis. The scheme forms 13 signed combinations of the entries of A and 14 of B, takes 23 products, and recombines them with 28 further additions; its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4. The previous records, from 60 down to 56, were obtained by greedy common-subexpression elimination, which only bounds each side of a scheme from above. We minimize both input sides exactly by chain covering, and the output side exactly through the transposition principle: the 9-by-23 output map costs its transpose plus 14, and the transpose is a 9-input map that the input-side minimizer solves exactly. Applied to Perminov's cn122 scheme (class i19w225c4efh, published at 58 additions) this gives 55 = 13 + 14 + 28, where greedy elimination reaches only 29 on the output side. The same method shows that Sun's representative is output-optimal at 56, and an exact orbit-wide computation over the Heule-Kauers-Seidl database shows that the record class is the only database class attaining 55.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 11 pages. Artifacts (program, verifier, Lean 4 proof): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21240904; source: https://github.com/gsidebottom/logic

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximating Directed Telephone Multicast
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the telephone model a message starts at a source vertex, and in every round each informed vertex may call one neighbour. Telephone multicast asks for a schedule that informs a given set of $k$ terminals in the fewest rounds. On directed graphs, the best known ratio for this problem was $\tilde O(\sqrt k)$, due to Elkin and Kortsarz and to Hathcock, Kortsarz and Ravi.
  For every integer $\ell\ge2$, we give a deterministic combinatorial algorithm with running time $n^{O(\ell)}$ that computes a schedule of length $O(\ell^3\log k)\cdot(\mathrm{OPT}+k^{1/\ell})$, where $n$ is the number of vertices and $\mathrm{OPT}$ the optimum. Since $\mathrm{OPT}\ge\log_2(k+1)$, this gives ratio $O(k^ε)$ in time $n^{O(1/ε)}$ for every fixed $ε>0$, and ratio $O(\log^4k)$ in quasi-polynomial time. The method rests on jump trees with additive vertex loads, a height reduction that bounds the load of every vertex, and a recursive greedy algorithm with an exponential potential. We also show that directed multicast is a special case of the degree-bounded directed Steiner tree problem on a time-expanded digraph. With known algorithms for that problem this gives randomized ratios $O(\log^2n)$ in time $n^{O(\log n)}$ and $O(n^ε)$ in time $n^{O(1/ε)}$, which, unlike ours, grow with $n$.
  On the hardness side, directed multicast stays $(1-ε)\ln k$-hard even when $\mathrm{OPT}=O(\log k)$, the regime in which the previous algorithms were weakest.

Graphics.title: WorldStream: Streaming Interactive 3D Worlds with Hierarchical Planning and Persistent State
Graphics.summary: We present WorldStream, an open-ended 3D world model with three simultaneous capabilities: it extends playable terrain beyond any pre-specified map, acts on open-ended language in the running world, and restores visited places with their edits. A hierarchical planner over a typed decision model emits structured decision state: Macro fixes settlement, ecology, transport, and hydrological structure across a group of tiles; Micro specializes that contract into tile semantics under measured terrain and accepted neighbor commitments. Deterministic local code compiles accepted plans into terrain, roads, settlements, vegetation, and entities. Streaming separates their reach: plans run ahead along the predicted corridor, compilation only where movement will soon need it, geometry behind the user released. One world record retains plans, seeds, object identities and mutable state, boundary commitments, and edits by attribute, revised as the user advances and edits; returning tiles recompile from it. The same record grounds interaction: the model acts on existing entities, including stateful NPCs that update as they act, edits the present region, or attaches intent to unplanned regions. Together they yield a world expanding under bounded budgets, connected across independently planned tiles, and interactive.

Graphics.title: Joints, Camera, Action! Co-Generating 3D Motion and Video for Arbitrary Rigs
Graphics.summary: Video generation models can now depict remarkably realistic motion. Yet it is unclear how to use this motion beyond pixels: to animate a specific 3D asset and replay the animation in its 3D scene. For instance, a video model can show a monkey jumping over a crossbar, but it cannot return that jump as replayable 3D motion placed in the 3D scene. Here we present a model that directly co-generates the video and 3D motion for any supplied rig, along with a camera that registers this motion to the scene. Prior video-motion models either handle only human skeletons, often adding billions of parameters, or triangulate 3D motion from generated 2D pose maps. We instead keep 3D motion in a separate model that supports arbitrary skeletons, and connect it to a pretrained video model through a small set of cross-attention layers. This separation lets the motion model first learn how skeletons move from motion-only data, which is easier to obtain and augment than paired video. Additionally, our model learns to locate each joint in the video frames, which lets us recover the camera and place the 3D motion in the scene. To train across many skeletons, we use a generative video editor to place animated 3D assets in scenes suited to their actions, curating the edits so their known motion remains valid. Together with human and robot video, this yields nearly 200K training pairs. Our evaluations demonstrate that our model animates diverse rigs from text more faithfully than video-first pipelines, and its motion responds to the surrounding scene. It also turns video into rig motion, rig motion into video, and enables keyframe-based control of the 3D motion. Videos and additional results are available on our project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/par/projects/jca/.

Graphics.title: Learning Adaptable Dexterous Skills via Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking
Graphics.summary: Dexterous multi-finger hands hold promise to unlock diverse skills like functional grasps, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic handover that the human-designed world assumes, yet existing learning recipes force a trade-off. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning generalizes to arbitrary object poses but, lacking any human prior, converges to unnatural and unreliable finger strategies; motion tracking reproduces human-like behavior from a single clip but cannot deviate from it. We present AdaDex, a goal-conditioned RL framework that turns a single hand-object trajectory of a few seconds---from mocap data or HOI reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video---into an adaptable dexterous skill. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking: a shared policy is trained on two populations of massively parallel environments: motion tracking environments trained with dense motion tracking objective, which instill the human prior from human motion; and generalization environments with noised initial states and goals and a sparse object-success reward, which force the skill to work far off the reference. From seconds of human motion per skill, the resulting policies can learn diverse adaptable dexterous skills, such as functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Our method outperforms baselines in terms of generalization and functionality, and we demonstrate transfer across simulators and to the real world. Project page: https://yuxuank.com/AdaDex/.

Graphics.title: Neural Implicit Energy Optimization for LiDAR Mapping
Graphics.summary: Neural implicit representations provide memory-efficient signed distance field (SDF) parameterizations for large-scale LiDAR scenes, but the geometry recovered from sparse and often noisy inputs carries jitter and artifacts. Classical geometric optimization techniques resolve such artifacts with surface energy functionals, whose minimizers correspond to smooth surfaces. Motivated by this principle, we formulate neural LiDAR mapping as the optimization of energy functionals over the parameter space of neural implicit representations. Specifically, we regularize the signed distance field with an energy functional defined on the shape operator of its level set, which represents the curvature of the surface, thus encouraging smoothness along the surface. This adapts classical geometric priors to the scale of million-point LiDAR maps. Experiments on large-scale datasets show reconstructions with improved smoothness at preserved geometric fidelity, and no additional inference-time cost. The code is publicly available at \href{https://github.com/HrishikeshVish/nieo}{https://github.com/HrishikeshVish/nieo}

Graphics.title: Gibson Env: Real-World Perception for Embodied Agents
Graphics.summary: Developing visual perception models for active agents and sensorimotor control are cumbersome to be done in the physical world, as existing algorithms are too slow to efficiently learn in real-time and robots are fragile and costly. This has given rise to learning-in-simulation which consequently casts a question on whether the results transfer to real-world. In this paper, we are concerned with the problem of developing real-world perception for active agents, propose Gibson Virtual Environment for this purpose, and showcase sample perceptual tasks learned therein. Gibson is based on virtualizing real spaces, rather than using artificially designed ones, and currently includes over 1400 floor spaces from 572 full buildings. The main characteristics of Gibson are: I. being from the real-world and reflecting its semantic complexity, II. having an internal synthesis mechanism, "Goggles", enabling deploying the trained models in real-world without needing further domain adaptation, III. embodiment of agents and making them subject to constraints of physics and space.
Graphics.comment: Access the code, dataset, and project website at http://gibsonenv.stanford.edu/ . CVPR 2018 (spotlight)

Graphics.title: Learning from Automatic 3D Gaussian Splatting Edits for Online Bayesian Scene Change Detection
Graphics.summary: Online scene change detection requires integrating incoming observations to determine which regions have changed relative to a reference scene. We update change beliefs as new images arrive using generalised Bayesian evidence fusion. However, the prior probability of change and evidence models are unknown beforehand, and numerical Bayesian inference can be costly. We address these challenges by learning offline from automatic edits to a reference 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. These edits generate labelled training views without manual annotations. Together with unchanged reference observations, they provide supervision for learning scene-specific evidence models and estimating the effective pixel prior and response statistics. Online prediction combines current evidence with historical support, while closed-form local Bayes factors, parameterized by the learned response statistics, update an accumulated 3D Gaussian field. Object-guided refinement produces the final change masks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on PASLCD and CCS3D, with $67.64\%$ and $75.82\%$ mIoU, respectively. On PASLCD, the complete pipeline runs at $17.2$\,FPS over complete query sequences, the fastest among the evaluated online methods.

Graphics.title: GALA: Geometry-Aware Language Model for Controllable Object Arrangement
Graphics.summary: Reasoning about fine-grained placement constraints, such as support and containment, is essential for realistic 3D scene creation. It remains a significant challenge for existing methods that rely on simplified object representations like oriented bounding box (OBB), which are blind to the detailed geometry. To address this limitation, we introduce GALA, a geometry-aware language model with explicit point cloud perception for controllable object placement. Our model performs autoregressively by predicting the 6D pose of one target object at a time conditioned on the scene context and placement instruction. We utilize a two-stage training strategy: the first stage aligns geometric and textual modalities through pretraining tasks, and the second stage fine-tunes the model for placement. To facilitate this task, we also curate a multi-source scene dataset covering diverse room types and fine-grained furniture arrangements, which will be open-sourced for community benefit. Experiments on our benchmark show our model significantly outperforms baselines without explicit geometric reasoning. We further develop a multi-stage plan-place-verify agent pipeline that uses the model for text-driven scene generation. Project Page: https://xccelephant.github.io/paper/gala/
Graphics.comment: Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers. Project Page: https://xccelephant.github.io/paper/gala/

Graphics.title: Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer
Graphics.summary: A geometric style learned from one family of shapes is typically applied to new shapes from the same family. We consider a more challenging setting: learning the geometric design language of a stylized Latin alphabet and applying it to new forms, from Greek glyphs to entirely different structures such as human poses. We introduce Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed. This setting is deceptively challenging: the difficulty is not merely learning a style, but learning the style without learning the shape family in which it was observed. We represent target forms by structural sketches and disentangle structural adherence from style realization using a Geometry LoRA and a style-specific LoRA. Critically, open-form transfer requires the Geometry LoRA to be universal. To achieve this, we devise a geometry-enrichment strategy that constructs a large and purposefully diverse collection of synthetic structural sketches spanning a broad range of unfamiliar geometries. Our experiments and ablations demonstrate the importance of both disentanglement and this universal geometry prior, enabling geometric styles learned from glyphs, pictograms, and other shape families to be transferred to substantially different, unseen forms.

Graphics.title: PocketGS: High-Fidelity On-Device Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting
Graphics.summary: Although 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) supports real-time rendering, training relies on offline geometry, long-horizon densification, and memory-intensive differentiation. We cast post-capture static-scene training as resource-constrained finite-horizon optimization, where terminal quality depends jointly on the initial representation and reference-consistent gradient execution. To the best of our knowledge, PocketGS is the first publicly documented pipeline to complete geometry construction, Gaussian initialization, and 3DGS optimization on a commodity smartphone. Its I, G warm start combines refined poses, a filtered dense prior, and surface-aligned anisotropic Gaussians. Its T operator replays compositing interactions and scatters gradients to canonical parameters, matching a numerical reference at the reported precision. Controlled 500-step experiments on LLFF, Mip-NeRF 360, and MobileScan show high-quality reconstruction at the device horizon. Across MobileScan, every scene remains below 3 GB peak memory and post-capture processing averages 255.2 s, enabling an on-device capture-to-render workflow. Separate 30k experiments characterize native-schedule behavior.

Graphics.title: OV-Foam: How 3D Representations Shape Semantic Feature Lifting
Graphics.summary: Existing feature lifting approaches for open-vocabulary segmentation rely on simple backprojection to assign features to primitives. In the case of 3D Gaussian splatting reconstruction, the primitives overlap heavily, leading to suboptimal reconstructions, governed by many primitives per ray. Backprojection, however, reduces to a least-squares solvable problem, exactly when no two primitives share a ray. Motivated by this insight, we propose OV-Foam, which uses PowerFoam as the underlying representation. This representation uses a power-diagram to partition the scene, resulting in zero overlap between primitives and a substantial reduction in primitives per ray, which ultimately simplifies the lifting problem and allows for closer-to-optimal feature assignment. We show that the space partitioning primitives of OV-Foam reach near-optimal assignment, and our experiments demonstrate improved open-vocabulary segmentation over Gaussian baselines.

Graphics.title: A Process-Informed, Photorealistic Digital Twin for Vision-Based Inline Inspection of C-SMC Strip Deposition
Graphics.summary: Inline quality assurance for Sheet Molding Compound (SMC) manufacturing is hindered by the lack of large-scale, accurately labeled image datasets for training machine-learning models. This work presents a process-informed, photorealistic digital twin for carbon-fiber SMC strip deposition. A rigid-body simulation reproduces the deposition kinematics (settling, friction, belt motion), while a physically grounded polarization-rendering model produces realistic appearance, so that every image carries exact, mutually consistent labels in synchronized formats: oriented bounding boxes, point annotations, density maps, and polarization renderings (Angle and Degree of Linear Polarization). Because the joint distribution of many overlapping strips cannot be specified analytically, simulation yields exact, scalable ground truth that manual annotation cannot provide. The twin produces over 16,000 images across 3,300 frames, and the synthetic data replicate near-isotropic fiber orientation (axial concentration r < 0.05) consistent with as-deposited commercial SMC. Trained purely on synthetic data, YOLOv11 and CSRNet reach detection mAP50 up to 0.91, with a dedicated oriented-bounding-box detector confirming the oriented labels are directly trainable (mAP50 = 0.83); on real manufacturing images, the synthetic-to-real difference in edge and texture structure (Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance 0.46, distribution overlap 0.56) is of the same magnitude as the difference between two real acquisition series of the same material (0.41, overlap 0.57). The approach substantially reduces the labeling burden for camera-based inline inspection of fiber orientation and volume content.
Graphics.comment: 46 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to Composites Part A: Applied Science and Manufacturing

Graphics.title: Dancing Diffusion: Learning Continuous Programs for Image Generation and Editing
Graphics.summary: Diffusion models generate samples through a multi-step denoising trajectory, yet condition every step on the same instruction, so the trajectory cannot be addressed at the level of individual operations. We introduce Dancing Diffusion, which assigns each span of timesteps a dedicated continuous condition block and thereby turns conditioning into a latent program. A compiler maps text features into this program, and a fixed pretrained generator executes its blocks over successive sampling intervals. The trajectory can then dance, keeping its executed history while its continuation is redirected. A shared prefix is executed once and reused, and a later operation is rewritten while content fixed by earlier operations is preserved. The compiler is trained through the images it produces, with visual feedback on both the requested change and the retained content. On SANA, reusing an executed prefix preserves markedly more of the scene than regenerating from noise at a similar strength of edit, learned conditions preserve more background than native prompt switching from the same saved state, and the learned program improves generation quality over native SANA. Later branches weaken the edit, which leaves semantic control over individual operations limited. By converting a single-instruction trajectory into a program of addressable operations, Dancing Diffusion lays a foundation for structured intermediate computation in diffusion models.

Graphics.title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Harnessing Video Models for Real-Time Playable Game Worlds
Graphics.summary: Moving from controllable videos to genuinely playable worlds requires persistent world state, executable game rules, and low-latency interaction. We outline a roadmap for the next generation of Matrix-Game that separates game execution from visual generation through an executable game harness, and introduce Matrix-Game 4.0 as the first system built on this design. A lightweight game engine maintains world state and executes interaction rules, a multimodal coding agent translates player ideas into game code and dynamic scene captions, and a renderer based on autoregressive video model transforms engine-rendered low-poly proxies into detailed visuals, conditioned on dynamic captions and memory references. This framework provides continuous guidance for visual generation and enables natural-language creation and modification of scenes and gameplay. Our renderer is trained on aligned low-poly and high-fidelity video pairs and distilled into a causal generator that generates in four-frame chunks with one or two denoising steps. Together with targeted inference optimizations, Matrix-Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX5090 with a key-press-to-display latency of 112ms. Single-step generation achieves 83FPS steady-state throughput with 18.2GiB of peak GPU memory usage. With fixed prompts, steady-state throughput also reaches 67FPS on an RTX5080 and 58FPS on an RTX5070Ti. We demonstrate customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics, and release code, model weights, and low-poly game assets to support research and creation of playable game worlds.
Graphics.comment: Project page, videos, code and models: https://matrix-game-v4-0.github.io/page/

Graphics.title: Geometry Regularization for Vanilla NeRF via Self-Supervised Cross-Ray Consistency
Graphics.summary: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve high-quality novel-view synthesis by representing a scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field. However, the geometry encoded by the density field of vanilla NeRF can be noisy and inaccurate, since different combinations of shape and radiance may explain the same input images. To reduce this ambiguity, we augment vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch based on self-supervised cross-ray consistency. Specifically, this branch samples candidate surface points from the density field, generates virtual rays that intersect at each point from different directions, and renders their appearance using the NeRF network. Based on the visibility-weighted color consistency across these rays, we constrain the implicit geometry. We further regularize the implicit geometry by penalizing opacity at candidates with inconsistent appearance predictions and encouraging local normal smoothness. These geometric constraints are derived from the NeRF predictions and require no ground-truth depth or surface-normal supervision. Experiments on eight Replica scenes show that the proposed method reduces the mean Chamfer distance by 30.8% compared with vanilla NeRF.

Graphics.title: Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production
Graphics.summary: We present Stable Signer V3, an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting. It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. Shared Face Primitive Splatting adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details. Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters. Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.

Graphics.title: PartLLM: A Unified Multimodal Foundation for 3D Part Segmentation
Graphics.summary: Part segmentation is a fundamental problem in computer graphics and 3D vision. Recent works have expanded 3D part segmentation beyond fixed taxonomies, but existing approaches typically only address a specific setting, such as text-guided part segmentation or point-based interaction. In this work, we argue that these settings can be unified as an intent-conditioned generative problem, where different prompts specify the desired part decomposition. To this end, we introduce PartLLM, a unified multimodal model that formulates 3D part segmentation as autoregressive semantic decomposition. Conditioned on an input shape and a user prompt, PartLLM autoregressively generates semantic part hypotheses as queries for mask prediction and feeds them to a decomposition-aware decoder that jointly predicts coherent part masks. This unified design supports text-guided part segmentation, interactive segmentation, and full-shape semantic decomposition with controllable granularity within a single model. Extensive experiments across these task settings show that PartLLM consistently outperforms task-specific baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of unifying 3D part segmentation under an intent-conditioned generative formulation.
Graphics.comment: Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 (ACM Transactions on Graphics). Project Page: https://czvvd.github.io/PartLLMPage/

Graphics.title: SwitchSplat: Learning Discrete Object States from Casually Captured Scenes
Graphics.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world. This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment -- opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects -- introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model. Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate when a state was observed with what state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations. We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base+slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object. Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation. At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io
Graphics.comment: SIGGRAPH Asia 2026. 21 pages, 18 figures, 10 tables. v2 adds two sections in suppl.: A.9 Training on Native Fisheye Frames and A.10 Automatic Mask-Guided Slot Refinement

Graphics.title: Test-time Adaptation for Point Cloud Denoising under Unseen Noise
Graphics.summary: Although deep learning-based point cloud denoising methods have demonstrated impressive results in recent years, their effectiveness usually degrades substantially in real-world scenarios where the noise distribution of test point clouds deviates from that of the training set. To address this challenge, we propose a test-time adaptive denoising (TTAD) framework that enables existing denoising approaches to adapt to unknown noise patterns at test time without relying on additional supervision or retraining from source data. Taking a pre-trained denoising model and a test noisy point cloud as input, TTAD first employs a residual-driven noise modeling (RDNM) module to estimate the sample-specific noise distribution through analyzing the deviation between the noisy input and its pseudo-clean version denoised by the initial model. Then, a noise-aware contrastive adaptation (NACA) module is designed to build sample-specific noisy-noisier test-time training pair from the denoised point cloud, and update the model parameters over a few adaptation steps per sample at test time through contrastive learning. Furthermore, TTAD naturally extends to a continual TTAD (CTTAD) setting, facilitating efficient progressive refinement across sequential test samples with consistent noise distributions, while reducing the computational cost per sample. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the generalization ability of existing denoising models under unseen noise, achieving superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics.

Operating Systems.title: SARIA: Persistence-Aware KV Caching with Coordinated DRAM--SSD Reload for LLM Agents
Operating Systems.summary:
Multi-turn LLM agents usually reuse long context prefixes, making key value (KV) caching crucial for reducing prefill latency. SSDs provide a low-cost extension to limited DRAM capacity but introduce two key challenges. Eagerly persisting all KV cache blocks incurs substantial write traffic and rapidly consumes finite SSD endurance. Meanwhile, the small number of SSDs provisioned in typical GPU servers limits aggregate reload bandwidth, making SSD-resident KV cache much slower to retrieve than that in DRAM and inflating prefill latency.
  We present \textsc{Saria} (Selective Admission and Reload for Inference Acceleration), a KV caching system that jointly manages DRAM and SSD by exploiting the session-level temporal locality of LLM agents to reduce SSD writes and accelerate cache reload. On the write path, \textsc{Saria} uses eviction and reuse history to selectively persist KV cache blocks that exhibit reuse opportunities beyond their DRAM residency, avoiding unnecessary writes for KV cache already hosted in DRAM. On the read path, \textsc{Saria} promotes selected SSD-hit KV cache blocks from GPU memory into DRAM after prefill, allowing subsequent reuse within the same session to reduce SSD read traffic while limiting DRAM contention. A transfer coordinator paces DRAM reads while SSD transfers are active, allowing both paths to make progress and efficiently share GPU ingress bandwidth.
  We implement \textsc{Saria} on LMCache MP and evaluate it using workloads from TraceLab and WEKA, covering both full-attention and hybrid-attention models. The results show that \textsc{Saria} reduces SSD writes by 57.1--58.9\% compared with popular full duplicate caching and the mean time to first token (TTFT) by 42.3--79.7\% over DRAM-only caching.

Operating Systems.title: uGDS: A User-Space Development Kit for High-Performance GPU Direct Storage
Operating Systems.summary:
Data-intensive GPU applications increasingly rely on NVMe SSDs to extend GPU memory. NVIDIA GPU Direct Storage (GDS) enables direct SSD-GPU transfers via PCIe peer-to-peer DMA, eliminating host staging. However, GDS retains three key limitations: (1) its control path traverses the kernel for every I/O request, introducing software overhead; (2) its stream-ordered path imposes strict total ordering even when workloads only require batch-level ordering; and (3) its closed-source user-space engine hinders diagnosis and custom scheduling.
  We present uGDS, https://github.com/ScaleX-IO/uGDS, an open-source user-space GPU Direct Storage library built on four principles: user-space control, unified cross-vendor abstraction, workload-aware scheduling, and end-to-end transparency. The host CPU manages the entire NVMe command lifecycle in user space, while payloads move via PCIe P2P DMA without consuming GPU compute. A minimal kernel module (ugds_drv.ko) is used only for one-time privileged setup. uGDS partitions hardware queues between synchronous and batch traffic, enforces DMA-safe buffer lifetimes, and provides cuFile-compatible synchronous, batched, and stream-ordered APIs with polling or interrupt completion on both NVIDIA CUDA and AMD HIP.
  Evaluated on an A100 with a Samsung 990 PRO, uGDS achieves up to 12.12x GDS's batch-read bandwidth and 30.69x its batch-write bandwidth (8- and 4-KiB requests, batch size 128), and reduces 4-KiB synchronous write latency by 84.1% with two threads. Its stream-ordered path sustains 5.49 GiB/s on a single stream, where GDS retains only 40.8% of its synchronous bandwidth. In LMCache, uGDS reduces median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by up to 62.7% and raises serving goodput by 2.63x. On AMD, uGDS achieves up to 1.19x hipFile's synchronous-write bandwidth.
Operating Systems.comment: 17 pages,16 figures, Technical report. Source code: https://github.com/ScaleX-IO/uGDS

Operating Systems.title: Breaking the Coupling: Efficient Concurrency Fuzzing for Linux Kernel Data Race Detection
Operating Systems.summary:
Detecting data races in the Linux kernel requires exploring both the input space and the thread-interleaving space. Existing kernel concurrency fuzzers couple these two searches by exploring interleavings during fuzzing, often spending substantial scheduling effort on inputs with little potential to trigger real races. In this paper, we present a new concurrency fuzzing paradigm that decouples concurrent-input generation from thread-interleaving exploration, enabling expensive scheduling to focus on promising inputs.
  To identify inputs that warrant targeted scheduling, we introduce May Race Pairs (MRPs), which represent conflicting memory-access pairs observed within a dynamically determined time threshold. Our framework first generates and executes concurrent syscall groups without controlled scheduling, collecting MRPs to guide further input mutation and identify schedule-worthy inputs. It then uses a separate scheduling instance to explore targeted interleavings and confirm real data races. To improve the effectiveness of both stages, we incorporate LLM-assisted semantic mutation for generating diverse syscall groups, backpressure-guided dynamic threshold control for balancing candidate production and scheduling consumption, and history-aware context recovery, context-aware interleaving scheduling, and candidate MRP prioritization for efficient race confirmation.
  We implement our framework for the Linux kernel and evaluate it on eight common kernel modules in Linux 6.17. It discovers 187 unique real-world data races, including 59 harmful races. Under the same testing budget, our approach detects substantially more data races than existing kernel concurrency fuzzers, including SegFuzz and CONZZER. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of decoupling concurrent-input generation from interleaving exploration and concentrating scheduling effort on promising candidates.

Hardware Architecture.title: Ray-by-Ray: Fine-Grained Resource Management for GPU Ray Tracing Units
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Ray tracing (RT) generates photorealistic images by simulating the physical behavior of light as it interacts with surfaces in a virtual scene. In film production and high-end rendering pipelines, this technique computes global illumination, reflections, refractions, and soft shadows by tracing millions of light rays per frame and accurately modeling their bounces and attenuation. Contemporary GPUs incorporate specialized ray tracing hardware to accelerate key operations in the traversal pipeline. By accelerating these stages in hardware, the unit enables real-time ray tracing for complex scenes that previously required offline computation. However, ray tracing introduces substantial control and data divergence. Each ray may traverse a different set of nodes in the acceleration structure, encounter distinct materials, or terminate at varying depths. This irregularity reduces thread coherence and exposes a fundamental disparity between the GPU SIMT and per-thread execution model of dedicated RT units, where each ray progresses independently.
  In this work, we seek to validate assumptions made in open-source infrastructure and identify potential inefficiencies in resource management within the ray tracing pipeline. To address inefficiency caused by mismatches between SIMT and RT granularities, we propose Ray-by-Ray, which decomposes on-chip buffers into the granularity of individual rays and introduces lightweight management structures that enable more warps to run in parallel without increasing buffer capacity. This approach improves ray tracing unit utilization and increases memory-level parallelism. Experimental results show that Ray-by-Ray achieves an average performance improvement of 1.91x over the baseline, with an area overhead of 0.19\%.
Hardware Architecture.comment: to be published in 59th IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture

Hardware Architecture.title: ARES: Adaptive Reasoning-Effort Steering for PPA- and Cost-Aware RTL Optimization with LLM Agents
Hardware Architecture.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents optimize the power, performance, and area (PPA) of register-transfer-level (RTL) designs by iterating over edits, synthesis, and PPA analysis, paying a dollar cost for every LLM call. Prior agents report the quality reached without its normalized cost, attribute that quality to an engineered cross-design memory, and hold the reasoning effort of every call fixed. We propose Ares with three corresponding innovations. (1) We introduce a normalized dollar cost per LLM call reported alongside the figure of merit (FoM), enabling fair comparison across effort levels and optimizers. (2) Using this accounting, we find the construction of the long-term memory matters little. An engineered memory brings no dependable gain over a plain concatenation of the same experience. (3) We instead adapt the per-call reasoning effort by escalating to deeper reasoning only once progress at a lower effort stalls, via a patience counter fit on 21 training designs, allocating reasoning where it pays rather than uniformly across all iterations. On three test designs unseen during training, the effort policy lowers the FoM by 22-28% with Opus 4.6 and by 18-34% with GPT-5.5, where the best fixed effort reaches 20-24% and 19-29%, respectively, at equal normalized cost. Ares closes on average 91% of the gap from an LLM-drafted multiply-accumulate unit to its highly hand-optimized counterpart. It also reaches a 5% lower FoM than state-of-the-art Dr. RTL at only 35% of its cost.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 8 pages, 6 figures

Hardware Architecture.title: SnakeCharmer: Orchestrating Utility, Timeliness, and Placement in GPU Prefetching
Hardware Architecture.summary:
GPUs rely on massive thread-level parallelism to tolerate long memory latency, yet they still suffer severe stalls when many warps simultaneously wait for data from the memory system. Address-prediction-based GPU prefetchers can mitigate such stalls, but accurate prediction alone does not guarantee performance improvement: a predicted prefetch becomes beneficial only if it is worth issuing, arrives at the right time, and is retained without harmful interference. Because these requirements interact, optimizing any single dimension in isolation can simply move the bottleneck to another.
  We capture these requirements with a predicted-prefetch-to-realized-benefit perspective and propose SnakeCharmer, a unified backend prefetch-control framework for address-prediction-based GPU prefetchers. SnakeCharmer separates address prediction from prefetch realization: the frontend predictor generates prefetch candidates, while the backend control path jointly controls utility, timeliness, and placement by determining whether each candidate should be issued, when it should be issued, and where the returned data should be retained. SnakeCharmer realizes this control path with zero-value-aware filtering for utility, hierarchical feedback-driven distance tuning for timeliness, and a register-assisted prefetch buffer for placement. We design and implement SnakeCharmer primarily on top of Snake, and adapt the same backend-control principles to APOGEE to demonstrate that SnakeCharmer's benefits are not limited to a single frontend predictor. On an A100 GPU model, SnakeCharmer improves performance/energy efficiency by 12.8%/20.8% over Snake and by 1.7%/3.2% over APOGEE, with modest hardware overhead.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 15 pages, 26 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 59th IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO 2026)

Hardware Architecture.title: Hard and Soft Real-Time DNN Inference Scheduling on Heterogeneous Multi-Accelerator Systems via Reinforcement Learning
Hardware Architecture.summary:
We present a scheduling framework for heterogeneous multi-accelerator systems executing both hard real-time and soft real-time QoS-aware DNN inference workloads. The framework combines an online reinforcement learning (RL) scheduler with a deterministic runtime safety layer. The RL scheduler dynamically generates candidate schedules by jointly selecting sub-job priorities and accelerator assignments, while runtime certification guarantees that all HRT deadlines remain satisfied independently of the learned policy.
  To enable runtime certification in heterogeneous precedence-constrained systems, we introduce a schedulability-preserving prefix replacement criterion based on machine-wise cuts. The proposed criterion guarantees that runtime-generated schedule prefixes preserve the existence of a feasible continuation without requiring complete finish-time dominance with respect to a feasible reference schedule.
  Experimental results on heterogeneous DNN accelerator platforms show that the proposed framework preserves HRT schedulability while improving QoS-aware deadline satisfaction, client-level service quality, and accelerator utilization compared to state-of-the-art scheduling approaches.
Hardware Architecture.comment: This paper has been accepted for presentation at the 34th International Conference on Real-Time Networks and Systems (RTNS 2026)

Hardware Architecture.title: HDLouvain: High-Throughput Incremental Clustering for Hyperdimensional Data
Hardware Architecture.summary: Modern shotgun proteomics generates tens of thousands of tandem mass spectra per hour, producing hundreds of gigabytes of data that strain conventional clustering pipelines. DBSCAN and hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC) offer flexible similarity search, but DBSCAN is unstable across varying data densities, HAC costs $O(n^2)$, and both yield poor cluster quality. Graph-based methods such as Louvain produce high-quality clusters but scale poorly on streaming data. We observe that Louvain's poor scalability can be resolved without sacrificing its quality, and present HDLouvain, which combines Louvain community detection with the bit-parallel similarity computation of hyperdimensional computing (HDC). HDLouvain partitions a bootstrap fraction of the stream into precursor-mass buckets, applies Louvain to each bucket's kNN similarity graph, and condenses each community into a single binary hypervector by bitwise-majority bundling rather than iterative centroid recomputation. New spectra are assigned by a GPU-accelerated Hamming distance lookup against representatives in their mass bucket, or seed a new cluster when no match meets a similarity threshold $τ$, so the partition grows incrementally without full re-clustering. On five PRIDE datasets (0.99M to 21.13M spectra), sweeping the bootstrap fraction $α$ from 0.2 to 0.9 exposes an explicit, monotonic throughput-fidelity trade-off. On PXD003258, speedup ranges from 4.5x at $α=0.3$ to 1.65x at $α=0.7$. Modularity rises from 0.75-0.76 at $α=0.2$ to 0.95-0.97 at $α=0.9$, never more than 8% below full static recomputation. The Louvain stage achieves 0.86-0.93 normalized mutual information (NMI) on LFR benchmark networks with 30k to 2M nodes, whereas DBSCAN and HAC degrade to 0.57.

Programming Languages.title: A Multi-Dimensional, Per-Pass Empirical Study of the LLVM Optimization Pipeline
Programming Languages.summary: Quantifying the marginal impact of individual optimization passes underpins phase ordering, pass selection, optimization design, and analysis of pass/hardware interactions. In LLVM, the standard backend for C/C++, Rust, and ML stacks via MLIR, interactions among passes, measurement noise, and pipeline scale make this difficult. We present a systematic empirical study of the LLVM -O3 pipeline. We decompose it into 113 cumulative per-pass prefixes and measure execution time, compile time, binary size, hardware counters, and RAPL energy on 30 PolyBench/C kernels (84,750 measurements). Transitions whose binary is byte-identical to their predecessor give us a built-in null distribution, which we use to calibrate every significance claim. On these compute-bound affine kernels, the pipeline is non-monotone: 36% of the transitions that significantly change runtime are regressions, found in 28 of 30 kernels. Gains are back-loaded (the median kernel needs 84.8% of the pipeline for 80% of its speedup) and concentrated in a small core of passes, a result that holds under both absolute and scale-free impact measures. IR instruction count is an unreliable runtime predictor, and runtime-targeted passes are de facto energy-targeted (30-60% savings). Finally, we bound the speedup lost to non-monotone behavior from above by 46.35% and decompose it: 9.7 points are measurement noise, 15.3 points are transient dips repaired within three passes, and only 21.3 points persist to the end of the pipeline. These findings inform pass pruning, cost-model calibration, and autotuning.
Programming Languages.comment: 12 pages, 8 figures

Programming Languages.title: Ohana trees, linear approximation and multi-types for the $λ$I-calculus: No variable gets left behind or forgotten!
Programming Languages.summary:
