Although the $λ$I-calculus is a natural fragment of the $λ$-calculus, obtained by forbidding the erasure of arguments, its equational theories did not receive much attention. The reason is that all proper denotational models studied in the literature equate all non-normalizable $λ$I-terms, whence the associated theory is not very informative. The goal of this paper is to introduce a previously unknown theory of the $λ$I-calculus, induced by a notion of evaluation trees that we call "Ohana trees". The Ohana tree of a $λ$I-term is an annotated version of its Böhm tree, remembering all free variables that are hidden within its meaningless subtrees, or pushed into infinity along its infinite branches.
  We develop the associated theories of program approximation: the first approach -- more classic -- is based on finite trees and continuity, the second adapts Ehrhard and Regnier's Taylor expansion. We then prove a Commutation Theorem stating that the normal form of the Taylor expansion of a $λ$I-term coincides with the Taylor expansion of its Ohana tree. As a corollary, we obtain that the equality induced by Ohana trees is compatible with abstraction and application.
  Subsequently, we introduce a denotational model designed to capture the equality induced by Ohana trees. Although presented as a non-idempotent type system, our model is based on a suitably modified version of the relational semantics of the $λ$-calculus, which is known to yield proper models of the $λ$I-calculus when restricted to non-empty finite multisets. To track variables occurring in subterms that are hidden or pushed to infinity in the evaluation trees, we generalize the system in two ways: first, we reintroduce annotated versions of the empty multiset indexed by sets of variables; second, (...)
Programming Languages.comment: This is the (submitted) long version of the (published) conference version v2, see https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.FSCD.2025.12

Programming Languages.title: Typed Template Fuzzing
Programming Languages.summary: Fuzzing software with complex inputs has been a longstanding challenge. Traditionally, fuzzers either programmatically encode language constraints, requiring significant engineering effort, or rely on users to declare grammars and constraints. Recent LLM-based fuzzers address these drawbacks but introduce new issues. Some use LLMs for test generation, sacrificing throughput and producing invalid inputs when the LLM makes mistakes. Others rely on language-specific parsers, static analysis, and AST manipulation libraries. We introduce Typed Template Fuzzing (TTF), a lightweight LLM-based fuzzing methodology. The key idea is to use LLMs in a preprocessing step to transform seeds into typed templates. The typed templates then enable semantically aware, mutation-based fuzzing without language-specific parsers, type checkers, or further LLM queries during fuzzing. By exploiting the correspondence between seeds and templates, TTF can moreover repair LLM mistakes. We have implemented TTF in our tool Typos, which we evaluate across 21 input languages, including C, C++, Go, Rust, SystemVerilog, Scala, and Java, as well as libraries such as PyTorch and Qiskit. In a six-month fuzzing campaign, we reported 135 bugs, 128 of which were previously unknown. Perhaps most notably, on average 96% of Typos's mutants are valid, coming close to the validity rates of domain-specific fuzzers. Our evaluation further shows Typos's benefits over the state of the art.

Programming Languages.title: The Reversible Intermediate Language L4, its Type System, and its Bidirectional Small-Step Semantics
Programming Languages.summary:
L4 is a generic, reversible, linearly-typed, low-level language intended as an intermediate language for compiling reversible programming languages to reversible machines. L4 is intended to replace and generalise RSSA, a reversible SSA form. Inspiration is drawn from other low-level reversible languages such as HSSA.
  In this paper, we define L4 first informally, and then give a formal type system and a bidirectional small-step semantics for L4: The rules have direction indicators to determine forwards or backwards execution, and the direction can be changed during execution.
Programming Languages.comment: 17 pages

Programming Languages.title: Structure-Aware Equivalence for Evaluating Autoformalized Statements
Programming Languages.summary:
Evaluating autoformalized mathematical statements requires determining whether a candidate preserves the mathematical claim intended by a trusted reference. Existing methods approach this problem from complementary directions: reference-free learned evaluators estimate semantic agreement but are not constrained to a formal equivalence relation, while reference-based proof methods typically employ whole-statement logical equivalence to provide formal certificates, which is too coarse for translation fidelity and may identify mathematically unrelated statements.
  We introduce Structure-Aware Equivalence (SAE), a role-preserving formal equivalence relation between syntactic and whole-statement logical equivalence that allows formally justified reformulations while preserving translation-relevant mathematical structure. We operationalize SAE in the Autoformalization Correctness Evaluator (ACE), which provides certified equivalence or inequivalence judgments and reports Inconclusive otherwise. On ProofNetVerif, a benchmark introduced with BEq+, ACE retains substantial equivalent-case coverage while remaining highly conservative in certifying disputed or inequivalent pairs. On targeted diagnostics, BEq+ accepts 94-96% of unrelated but whole-statement logically equivalent pairs, while Mathesis LeanScorer accepts 42% of localized meaning-changing perturbations; ACE accepts none of either set as equivalent.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Efficient and Optimal Learning of Discrete Distributions with Person-Level Privacy
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study learning a discrete distribution under person-level differential privacy in the batched setting. Given $n$ users, each contributing $m$ i.i.d. samples from an unknown distribution $μ$ over $[k]$, we seek an estimate of $μ$ with total-variation error $α$. We give polynomial-time algorithms under both pure and approximate differential privacy. Under pure $(\varepsilon,0)$-DP, we achieve $n = \widetilde O(k/(α^2 m)+k/(α\sqrt{m}\varepsilon)+k/\varepsilon)$, the first polynomial-time pure-DP guarantee matching the information-theoretic optimum up to logarithmic factors. Under approximate $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP, we achieve $n = \widetilde O(k/(α^2 m)+k/(α\sqrt{m}\varepsilon)+k+\log(1/δ)/\varepsilon)$. At $δ=2^{-Θ(k)}$, this is $\widetilde O(k)$ for fixed $α,\varepsilon,m$ and failure probability. Our algorithms use a new degree-6 sum-of-squares estimator for learning from untrusted batches. Its key ingredient is a trace-bounded diagonal majorizer for the difference between the empirical covariance of the repaired batch averages and the multinomial covariance predicted by their mean. We prove that clean data admit this certificate through semidefinite-programming duality and a new application of the stronger symmetric form of Grothendieck's inequality due to Friedland and Lim. The certificate preserves the mean-dependent variance of multinomial batch averages, yielding the near-optimal robust rate $O(η\sqrt{\log(1/η)/m})$ and providing the score required by the privacy reduction. We also prove a statistical query lower bound ruling out a uniformly smaller order of error under fixed polynomial SQ resource bounds.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Full version of the SODA 2027 paper

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Closing All-Exp Gaps in Local Search for the Traveling Salesman Problem and Maximum Constraint Assignment
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We prove the all-exp property for the Traveling Salesman Problem with the $2$-opt neighborhood, and for $(3,2,2)$- and $(2,3,2)$-Maximum Constraint Assignment with the flip neighborhood. The all-exp property states that infinitely many instances have an initial solution from which every sequence of improving moves to a local optimum, and hence every run of local search, has exponential length. For the Traveling Salesman Problem, the all-exp property was previously known for every $k$-opt neighborhood with $k \ge 3$, so our result for $2$-opt completes the picture for all $k$-kopt neighborhoods. In $(p,q,r)$-Maximum Constraint Assignment, each constraint involves at most $p$ variables, each variable occurs in at most $q$ constraints, and each domain has size $r$. Decreasing any of the parameters of $(3,2,2)$ or $(2,3,2)$ yields a problem in which every sequence of improving flips has polynomial length, so both Maximum Constraint Assignment results are tight. All three results settle long-standing open problems. Our proofs build on a common construction idea, which reveals a close connection between the local-search dynamics of the three problems.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Coresets for $k$-Means: When Does Uniform Sampling Suffice?
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Data summarization techniques, such as coresets, are essential for scaling clustering algorithms to massive datasets. We study uniform sampling, which is an extremely simple and ultra-efficient method to construct coresets, in the context of weak, stable, and strong coresets for the $k$-means problem in Hilbert space. We begin with the fundamental case $k=1$, and establish matching upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity of stable and weak coresets, finding that the two notions require different sample complexities. As a consequence, we obtain tight bounds for stable $1$-median coresets in $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ (and thus also Kendall--tau and Jaccard metrics), removing the dimension dependence of Carmel and Krauthgamer (ICLR 2026). Our analysis is substantially simpler than prior work and reduces to bounding the deviation of the sample mean. For the general $k$-means problem on $ρ$-separated instances, a well-studied structural assumption on the input, we show that uniform sampling yields a stable coreset for all $O(1)$-approximate solutions, and a strong coreset if the instance additionally has bounded kurtosis. In all these results, the sample complexity is independent of the dimension and the instance size.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Compressed Set Representations based on Set Difference
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We introduce a compressed representation of sets of sets that exploits how similar they are to each other. Our representation supports access, membership, predecessor and successor queries on the sets within logarithmic time. It also computes the support of any element (i.e., the sets containing it) in optimal time. In addition, we give a new MST-based construction algorithm for the representation that outperforms standard ones.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: journal version of a LATIN '26 paper

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Peak-Aware One-Way Trading: Competitive and Learning-Augmented Algorithms for Energy Procurement
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We introduce peak-aware one-way trading ($\texttt{PA-OWT}$), an online problem in which a player must purchase a fixed quantity of an asset by a deadline, minimizing its total cost plus a charge proportional to the largest single purchase at any time. The model is motivated by electricity procurement, where the cost of energy rewards buying at low prices, but peak demand charges discourage concentrating purchases in short periods. Balancing these incentives is challenging when future prices are unknown: a large purchase can establish a peak that later decisions cannot undo. We develop a peak-aware online algorithm that balances price and peak control with deadline feasibility and achieves the order-optimal competitive ratio. We further extend our results to a learning-augmented algorithm that uses predictions of optimal purchasing decisions to achieve an order-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff, exploiting accurate advice while retaining worst-case guarantees in the face of arbitrary prediction errors. Finally, we evaluate our algorithms in a case study on electricity procurement using historical electricity price traces to understand the benefits of peak-aware purchasing.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Pipelining vs. Combining in Aggregation Tasks
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the aggregation task (convergecast) in networks in the case that the values to be aggregated do not fit in a single message. We assume that every node starts with an input value, and there is an aggregation operator that is commutative, associative, and length-preserving, i.e., the result of aggregating two values has the same length as each of the input values. Since values do not fit in a message, they are transferred in a ``train'' of pipelined messages, which must be terminated whenever we want to aggregate values. The goal is to minimize the makespan time of aggregating all values. We present general lower bounds on the problem and optimal algorithms for several prevalent parallel computing architectures, including the hypercube and complete bipartite graphs, under both the splittable and unsplittable flows models. We also present an $O(\log n)$ approximation for general graphs in the unsplittable flows model.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Sharp Analysis of Fixed Offset Hash Tables
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We consider the class of open addressing hash tables that uses a fixed offset sequence $r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_{n-1}$ to find an open slot in the table. As special cases this subsumes linear probing ($r_i=i$) and quadratic probing ($r_i=i^2$).
  We give a simple analysis that the expected insertion time when the load factor is $1-ε$ is $O(ε^{-2})$. This bound is tight for linear probing (but not for quadratic probing), so the analysis cannot be improved at this level of generality.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Fast Approximation Algorithms for Balanced Edge and Vertex Separators
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We present a family of fast pseudo-approximation algorithms for the minimum balanced element cut problem in a graph, which includes vertex and edge separators. Given a graph $G=(V,E)$ with polynomially-bounded finite integer element weights with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, and a (constant) balance parameter $c\in(0,1/2)$, where $G$ has some (unknown) $c$-balanced element cut of size $OPT_c$, we give a (Monte-Carlo randomized) algorithm running in $O(n^{\varepsilon}m^{1+o(1)})$ time that produces a $Θ(1)$-balanced element cut of size $O(OPT_c\cdot\sqrt{(\log n)/\varepsilon})$ for any value $\varepsilon\in[Θ(1/\log(n)),Θ(1)]$.
  Our algorithms are based on a semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation of the problem. A standard approach to solving an SDP relaxation for this kind of problem would use the primal-dual Matrix Multiplicative Weights Update framework of Arora and Kale, but this framework does not seem to apply, since we cannot express all of our SDPs primal variables explicitly. Instead, we present a new MMWU framework for our problem that allows us to represent some of our variables implicitly. We also extend our framework to a general "Partial-variable MMWU framework", which we expect will be useful for future work. Our oracle for the balanced element cut problem within our framework uses $O(n^{\varepsilon}\text{polylog}(n))$ almost-linear time maximum-flow computations, and would be sped up if the time complexity of maximum-flow improves.
  For graphs with padding bound $β$, another oracle gives an $O(\sqrtβ/\varepsilon)$ approximation in $m^{1+o(1)}n^{\varepsilon}\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ time. It is known that $β\le O(\log h)$ for $K_h$-minor-free graphs (and in particular $β\le O(\log n)$).

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Exact Approximation Ratio of the Optimal Fixed-Price Mechanism in Bilateral Trade
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In bilateral trade, a seller owns an item that a buyer may value more, and their values are drawn independently from known distributions. A fixed-price mechanism posts a single price and trades exactly when both agents accept it. How much of the first-best expected welfare can the optimal fixed price guarantee? A sequence of analytic and computer-assisted results narrowed the worst-case ratio to the interval $[0.7292,0.73805]$, but its exact value remained open.
  We determine this ratio exactly: it equals $0.7380243357\ldots$, given in closed form through the unique root of an explicit one-dimensional equation. The guarantee holds for every pair of independent nonnegative distributions with finite means, including atomic and unbounded ones, and an explicit family of instances shows that no larger constant is possible.
  The proof reduces the problem, through put and call transforms of the two distributions and a worst-case choice of seller, to a one-dimensional control problem for the buyer. A logarithmic change of variables makes this problem strictly convex, so its first-order conditions certify a global optimum. The optimizer switches exactly once from an interior arc to the boundary and can be integrated in closed form. Realizing it yields a bounded seller and a bounded buyer together with a vanishing buyer atom at a diverging value. The worst case is approached by this family but attained by no instance.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Hardness and Approximation for Compressing Deterministic Finite Automata
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The delayed deterministic finite automaton ($\text{D}^2\text{FA}$) is a powerful tool for compressing the prohibitively large deterministic finite automata (DFAs) used in modern signature-based deep packet inspection systems. A $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$ augments a DFA with unlabeled default transitions to remove transitions that are similar. This technique works well in practice and has inspired numerous subsequent studies. However, existing approaches do not guarantee a $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$ of optimal size as they restrict the default transitions to form a forest. In this paper, we consider the problem of finding an optimal $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$. We make the key observation that cycles of default transitions can be valid and produce a smaller $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$, provided that for every character in the alphabet, at least one state in the cycle has an outgoing transition labeled by that character. This observation raises fundamental questions concerning the computational complexity of finding an optimal $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$ and the approximation guarantee of the standard (forest-restricted) approach. We answer both questions by showing that it is NP-hard to find an optimal $\text{D}^2\text{FA}$ and by proving that the standard approach provides a $3/2$-approximation to the optimum. To establish NP-hardness, we construct a reduction from set cover using a DFA with gadgets where valid default transition choices correspond to selecting sets. To prove our approximation ratio, we compare the cycles in an optimal solution to a variant where the default transitions form a forest. Finally, we demonstrate that this $3/2$ ratio is tight via a constructed family of DFAs.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 18 pages, 4 figures. Has been submitted for review

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Kempe Reachability with $k\geq 3$ Colors Is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-Complete on Claw-Free Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A \emph{proper vertex coloring} assigns colors to vertices so that adjacent vertices have distinct colors. A \emph{Kempe change} in a proper vertex coloring exchanges two colors on one component of the subgraph induced by the vertices of those colors. For a fixed palette of $k$ colors, \textsc{Kempe Reachability} asks whether two given proper vertex colorings of the same graph are connected by a sequence of Kempe changes. This problem is known to be $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete for every fixed $k\geq 3$. A graph is \emph{claw-free} if no vertex has three pairwise nonadjacent neighbors. The \emph{line graph} of a graph has one vertex for each edge, with two vertices adjacent exactly when the corresponding edges share an end. Line graphs are claw-free, and their Kempe changes correspond to \emph{edge-Kempe changes} in the original graph, which exchange two colors on one component of the subgraph formed by the edges of those colors. A claw-free graph with a proper $k$-coloring has maximum degree at most $2k-2$, whereas for $k\geq 4$ all proper $k$-colorings of a graph of maximum degree at most $k$ are connected by Kempe changes. We show that, for every fixed $k\geq 3$, \textsc{Kempe Reachability} with $k$ colors is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even on line graphs of connected simple $k$-regular graphs, and hence even on connected $(2k-2)$-regular claw-free graphs. Equivalently, deciding whether two proper $k$-edge-colorings are connected by edge-Kempe changes is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even on connected simple $k$-regular graphs.
  ChatGPT 6 Pro and Claude Fable 5.1 were used to assist with developing and reviewing mathematical arguments and drafting and revising the paper. The author takes full responsibility for the correctness and content of the paper.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for $k$-Path Vertex Cover Reconfiguration on Trees under Token Sliding
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A $k$-path vertex cover ($k$-PVC) of a graph is a set of vertices meeting every path on $k$ vertices. In Token Sliding, one token occupies each vertex of a cover; a move slides one token along an edge to an unoccupied vertex, preserving the cover property. We study whether two covers of a tree are joined by such moves. The case $k=2$ admits a linear-time decision algorithm. For every integer $k\geq2$, we give an $O(kn^2)$-time decision algorithm on trees of order $n$, with $k$ part of the input. Two covers are reachable precisely when their rigid tokens, which never move, occupy the same set and every component remaining after their deletion has the same token count. The proof transforms configurations of equal size without rigid tokens into a canonical configuration built on properly rooted subtrees, whose paths on $k$ vertices pass through their roots. A rooted-subtree recurrence identifies movable candidate tokens. We also give a direct recursive construction between the supplied endpoints, returning at most $8n^2\,3^{\lceil n/2\rceil}$ slides in $O(n^{10}3^{n/2})$ time.
  ChatGPT 6 Pro and Claude Fable 5.1 were used to assist with developing and reviewing mathematical arguments and drafting and revising the paper. The author takes full responsibility for the correctness and content of the paper.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Iterative Randomized Rounding for Better-Than-2 k-Median Approximation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the classic $k$-median problem and refine the iterative rounding framework recently introduced by Byrka, Guo, Hu, Li, Wan, and Wang [FOCS'26], which yields a $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation.
  Our algorithm opens $k+O(1)$ facilities and achieves an expected connection cost of at most $1.9999$ times the value of the standard LP relaxation. Although the numerical improvement over $2$ is small, it establishes a conceptual result: the integrality gap of the standard relaxation is strictly below $2$ when a constant number of extra facilities is allowed. This partially answers an open question of Li and Svensson [STOC'13]. Combined with their reduction, our result yields a $1.9999$-approximation algorithm for $k$-median.
  Our approach builds on several technical ingredients. First, we develop a preprocessing routine that makes the LP solution $\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)$-integral, at the cost of a $(1+\varepsilon)$ factor in the connection cost and $O(1)$ extra facilities. Unlike the preprocessing of Byrka et al. [FOCS'26], our conversion is unconditional: it requires no special treatment of clients whose fractional facilities are concentrated. Next, we show that the main rounding algorithm can open facilities one at a time, eliminating the batch processing used by Byrka et al. [FOCS'26]. Finally, the improvement over 2 comes from a tighter analysis for clients whose distances from to its facilities are not all equal, and a complementary algorithm for the case in which these distances are nearly uniform.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Fast and Compact Graph Cuts for the Boykov-Kolmogorov Algorithm
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Computing a minimum $s$-$t$ cut in a graph is a solution to a wide range of computer vision problems and is often done using the Boykov-Kolmogorov (BK) algorithm. In this paper, we revisit the BK algorithm from both a theoretical and practical point of view. We improve the analysis of the time complexity of the BK algorithm to $O(mn|C|)$ and propose a new algorithm, the fast BK (fBK) algorithm, with a time complexity of $O(m|C|)$, where $m$, $n$, and $|C|$ are the number of edges, the number of vertices, and the capacity of the cut, respectively. We additionally propose a compact graph representation that allows our implementations of the BK and fBK algorithms to find a minimum $s$-$t$ cut in a graph with up to $10^9$ vertices and $10^{10}$ edges on a machine with 128 GB of memory. We denote these as $\texttt{cBK}$ and $\texttt{fcBK}$, respectively. Despite $\texttt{fcBK}$ having the better worst-case guarantee, we find $\texttt{cBK}$ to be the fastest available implementation within the family of BK algorithms when evaluating on a comprehensive set of benchmark datasets, highlighting the importance of memory-efficient implementations. We make our implementations publicly available for further research and implementation development within minimum $s$-$t$ cut algorithms.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, submitted to the IEEE for possible publication

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Almost tight distributed approximation for domination in sparse graph classes
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study distributed approximation of Minimum Dominating Set in a very general class of sparse graphs, extending near-optimal approximation results from the minor-free setting to bounded expansion. In more detail, for fixed $d$ and $\varepsilon>0$, we give a new deterministic constant-round LOCAL algorithm for Minimum Dominating Set on graphs of maximum average degree at most $d$ and bounded depth-one shallow-minor density. Its approximation ratio is $d+1+\varepsilon$, which is optimal up to $\varepsilon$ for every even integer $d\geq 2$. This improves on the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz by extending beyond proper minor-closed classes. From this algorithm, we derive almost-tight constant-round approximations for a number of graph classes. We get $(7+\varepsilon)$-approximations for planar graphs and graphs of bounded Euler genus, and $(5+\varepsilon)$-approximations for their triangle-free subclasses. This answers the $7+\varepsilon$ question of Wawrzyniak positively, and matches the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz. We also apply our algorithm to classes of bounded queue-number or stack-number, obtaining bounds that are tight up to $\varepsilon$. Additionally, we answer questions of Amiri and Siebertz about improving the dependence of the round complexity on $1/\varepsilon$ and obtaining polynomial local computation for fixed parameters, when comparing the output to the usual domination number.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum: Subexponential Algorithm, Tight Lower Bounds, and Average-Case Analysis
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The Equal Subset Sum problem asks, given n positive integers bounded by M, to find two distinct non-empty subsets with the same sum. We study this problem in the regime $M = 2^{o(n)}$, where the pigeonhole principle guarantees that a solution exists, and the main challenge is to find one efficiently. A straightforward dynamic-programming algorithm runs in time poly(n).$M$. After a sequence of improvements, the current best algorithm, due to Jin, Williams, and Zhang (ESA 2025), achieves running time poly(n).$M^{1/3}$.
  In this work, we give the first poly(n).$M^{o(1)}$-time algorithm for Equal Subset Sum in the regime $M = 2^{o(n)}$. We complement this algorithmic result with a tight conditional lower bound showing that any substantial improvement would require a major breakthrough in approximation algorithms for lattice problems, building on recent techniques of Vafa and Vaikuntanathan (STOC 2025).
  Finally, we show that our techniques yield an asymptotically faster algorithm for the regime when $M = Θ(2^{n})$: a poly(n)$\cdot 2^{n/4}$-time algorithm in the average case.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Incremental Exact Vertex Connectivity
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the problem of maintaining the vertex connectivity $κ$ of a graph under edge insertions. For undirected graphs, our algorithm uses $O(κ^4 \log^2 n)$ amortized time per edge insertion. After each edge insertion, the algorithm outputs the current value of $κ$, plus a set of $κ$ vertices whose removal disconnects the graph. Our algorithm is Monte-Carlo randomized and works with a randomness-adaptive adversary. The algorithm also works on directed graphs against an oblivious adversary, which is equivalent to an output-adaptive adversary if we only have to output the current value of $κ$.
  Previously, algorithms using SPQR trees could maintain the vertex connectivity in undirected graphs with $O(\log n)$ time per edge insertion for $κ\le 3$, but no algorithm with $o(n)$ time per edge insertion was known for $κ\ge 4$. Moreover, for $κ\ge 4$, on general directed graphs or sparse undirected graphs, no algorithm faster than recomputation from scratch was known.
  We complement our algorithm with a conditional lower bound: Under the OMv conjecture, any insertions-only algorithm that outputs the current value of $κ$ after every insertion needs $Ω(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ amortized time per edge insertion for $κ= Θ(n)$. Previous conditional lower bounds for this problem only apply to worst case running time, or algorithms that support both edge insertions and edge deletions.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Truthful by Omission: Click Thinning for LLM-Native Advertising
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Generative AI assistants are becoming an advertising medium, embedding sponsored content in their answers. This setting departs from classical position auctions in two ways: an ad's click-through rate depends on the passage that hosts it, and because users stop at their first click, earlier ads take clicks from later ones. This competition for clicks makes truthfulness delicate: a higher bid can reshape the allocation and put a competitor ahead of the bidder, reducing the bidder's clicks. Existing mechanisms either attain a constant fraction of the optimal welfare (advertisers' total click value) but are not known to be truthful, or are truthful but their welfare guarantee degrades as the number of passages grows. We achieve both even when the answer and its editorial order are fixed before bidding. Assuming each ad's click-through rate when reached is known and unaffected by omitting other ads, we give a computationally efficient mechanism that is truthful in expectation and attains at least half the optimal welfare under free reordering.
  Our key idea, click thinning, omits ads at random, showing earlier ads less often so that each ad's overall click probability no longer depends on the order of the ads. Welfare maximization then reduces to a tractable matching problem, and solving it exactly with VCG-style payments makes truthful bidding optimal in expectation. Characterizing the click probabilities that omission can achieve sharpens the approximation factor from $2$ to $2-(1-δ)^{K-1}$ when at most $K$ ads are shown and each click-through rate is at most $δ$. This factor is the best possible for any order-preserving rule, even one that ignores incentives and computation, so truthfulness and computational efficiency incur no additional worst-case loss.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: NP-Completeness and ETH-Based Additive Inapproximability of Deterministic Communication Complexity via Relaxed Interlacing
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
How difficult is it to find an efficient communication protocol when the entire truth table of the function is given? We give a unified interlacing proof of NP-completeness for exact optimisation and of hardness of approximation. Assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis, there is a computable, nondecreasing additive error allowance tending to infinity for which approximation is impossible in polynomial time.
  The proof uses interlacing, which asks the players to solve one problem selected by Alice from a collection of inputs held by Bob. For suitable matrices, a short protocol must reveal enough of Alice's selection to encode a solution to a combinatorial problem. This produces a one-bit communication gap in a polynomial-size matrix and proves exact hardness. Repeating the construction is harder: earlier messages can remove the inputs on which a later lower bound depends.
  Restriction bounds that survive the construction make the one-bit gain repeatable. A smaller, balanced family of interlaced columns controls the truth-table size. For every fixed number of applications, the construction takes subexponential time in the source length. This rules out every fixed additive error under ETH. A general computability argument then yields the stated unbounded allowance.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 74 pages, 5 figures. Substantially revised and expanded from v4. Retains NP-completeness and adds ETH-based additive inapproximability: hardness for every fixed additive error and for one computable, nondecreasing unbounded allowance. Simplified exact-hardness proof; repeatable gap amplification with explicit truth-table size and running-time bounds

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Embeddability of hieroglyphs in the torus and the intersection form
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We characterize the hieroglyphs that embed in the torus, where a hieroglyph is a one-vertex graph with a rotation system. We prove equivalent criteria in terms of four forbidden hieroglyphs, the structure of the loop graph, reductions to three terminal forms, and the rank of the interlacement matrix. The proof uses the intersection form on the first homology of a disc with bands over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and the equality between its rank and twice the genus. We describe the effect of reductions and the role of boundary components. Counting the cycles of the boundary permutation yields a linear-time recognition algorithm for an indexed representation of the input.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 9 pages (English) + 10 pages (Russian); 8 figures in each language. English text followed by a Russian version. Proofs via the intersection form and a linear-time recognition algorithm

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Near-Quadratic Time Multivariate Polynomial Interpolation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Let $\F$ be a finite field. Given $N$ distinct points $\bmα_1,\ldots,\bmα_N \in \F^m$ and associated values $β_1,\ldots,β_N \in \F$, we study the problem of computing an $m$-variate polynomial $f(\vy) \in \F[\vy]$ of individual degree less than $d$, with $d^m \ge N$, that satisfies $f(\bmα_i)=β_i$ for all $i\in[N]$, whenever such an $f$ exists. This is known as the\textit{ multivariate polynomial interpolation} problem. In this work, given $N=d^m$, we present a deterministic algorithm for multivariate polynomial interpolation over an arbitrary finite field $\F$ that runs in near-quadratic time $N^{2+o(1)}\poly(m,d,\log|\F|)$, assuming $d$ is $ω(1)$. This bound holds whenever the associated \emph{multivariate Vandermonde} matrix is nonsingular, has constant co-rank, or admits some special structure. In the general case, we give a randomized Las Vegas algorithm attaining the same near-quadratic running time, provided the finite field is sufficiently large and $d$ grows similar to the previous case. Unlike other multivariate interpolation strategies, we do not assume black-box access to the polynomial. In particular, we are not permitted to query arbitrary input points to obtain their evaluations.
  Our interpolation result follows by combining Wiedemann's classical approach~\cite{w86} for solving sparse linear systems with known bounds for fast \emph{multivariate multipoint evaluation} over finite fields~\cite{umans08, KU11, BGKM23, BGGKU24}. Specifically, our deterministic interpolation strategy relies on a deterministic variant of Wiedemann's approach, which is more commonly used in the randomized setting.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimal-Time Move Structure Construction
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The move structure represents a permutation $π$ of $[0,n)$ by partitioning the domain into $O(r)$ disjoint, contiguously permuted intervals, with $r$ being the minimum number of such intervals. This data structure occupies $O(r)$ words of space and enables $O(1)$-time computation of $π(i)$ given the interval that contains $i$. For permutations where $r \ll n$, this provides an efficient, compressed representation for navigation. While the existing best $O(r)$-space construction approaches require $O(r\log r)$-time, we present an optimal $O(r)$-time and space construction algorithm. This is achieved by replacing balanced search trees with pointer-based lists through introducing a bidirectional strategy that synchronizes construction of the structures for $π$ and its inverse $π^{-1}$ in a single, unified pass. By applying this algorithm to an existing result, we achieve the first optimal $O(n)$-time construction of the longest common prefix (LCP) array from a run-length-encoded Burrows-Wheeler transform (RLBWT) of $r$ runs in $O(r)$ working space. Empirical evaluation on pangenome-scale data confirms that our move structure construction algorithm is consistently faster than the previous best, achieving speedups of up to $\sim 2\times$ while using less memory.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Power of Flexible Budgets in Adwords
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Search advertising platforms routinely spend beyond an advertiser's average daily budget on high-traffic days, so long as total spending over the month stays within the monthly budget. Motivated by this practice, we study a $D$-day generalization of the Adwords problem (Mehta et al. 2007), where each advertiser $i$ has a nominal (average) daily budget $B_i$ and a total horizon (monthly) budget $DB_i$. Given a flexibility parameter $δ$, the platform may spend at most $δB_i$ on advertiser $i$ on any single day, subject to the horizon spending limit of $DB_i$.
  We quantify the power of $δ$-flexible budgets by benchmarking against the inflexible offline optimum, which may spend at most $B_i$ on advertiser $i$ on each day. We show that no amount of flexibility helps direct generalizations of the classical algorithm of Mehta et al. (2007). By contrast, for every fixed $δ$, we design an algorithm whose competitive ratio converges to $1-e^{-δ}$ as $D\to\infty$, and we show that this is asymptotically optimal. Perhaps surprisingly, this matches the optimal competitive ratio in a more permissive setting where the algorithm receives a fresh spending limit of $δB_i$ each day and may spend up to $δD B_i$ over the horizon. Along the way, we characterize the exact optimal competitive ratio for every pair $(D,δ)$ on high-traffic instances, where the offline benchmark exhausts every advertiser's budget on every day.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimal Mixing for Local Edge-Coloring Dynamics on Trees
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the mixing time of two local Markov chains for uniformly sampling proper edge colorings of trees. For a tree with $n$ vertices and maximum degree $Δ$, we establish optimal mixing-time bounds for the single-edge Glauber dynamics when $q\geΔ+2$ and for the neighboring-edge heat-bath dynamics when $q\geΔ+1$. Both chains mix in $O_Δ(n(\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon)))$ steps, uniformly over the number of colors $q$. These bounds are tight in their dependence on $n$ for fixed $Δ$.
  Our proof establishes log-Sobolev inequalities through local color release, reusable recoloring buffers, and component entropy mixing. The two dynamics require different local constructions: a two-spare-color buffer for single-edge updates and a second-layer controller for neighboring-edge updates. The resulting entropy analysis applies to general bounded-degree trees, including regimes where worst-case spatial mixing fails.

Graphics.title: Dancing Diffusion: Learning Continuous Programs for Image Generation and Editing
Graphics.summary: Diffusion models generate samples through a multi-step denoising trajectory, yet condition every step on the same instruction, so the trajectory cannot be addressed at the level of individual operations. We introduce Dancing Diffusion, which assigns each span of timesteps a dedicated continuous condition block and thereby turns conditioning into a latent program. A compiler maps text features into this program, and a fixed pretrained generator executes its blocks over successive sampling intervals. The trajectory can then dance, keeping its executed history while its continuation is redirected. A shared prefix is executed once and reused, and a later operation is rewritten while content fixed by earlier operations is preserved. The compiler is trained through the images it produces, with visual feedback on both the requested change and the retained content. On SANA, reusing an executed prefix preserves markedly more of the scene than regenerating from noise at a similar strength of edit, learned conditions preserve more background than native prompt switching from the same saved state, and the learned program improves generation quality over native SANA. Later branches weaken the edit, which leaves semantic control over individual operations limited. By converting a single-instruction trajectory into a program of addressable operations, Dancing Diffusion lays a foundation for structured intermediate computation in diffusion models.

Graphics.title: H-2DGS: Height-Field Gaussian Splatting for Sharp and Deformable Neurosurgical Surface Reconstruction
Graphics.summary: Neurosurgical navigation commonly presents magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as 2D slices, making it difficult to relate the anatomy in those slices to the cortical surface observed through the surgical microscope. We seek a common 3D visualization that combines a photorealistic reconstruction of the exposed cortex during tumor surgery with whole-brain MRI context and diffusion tractography pathways. This requires the reconstructed cortex to form a clear boundary around the brain anatomy rather than a diffuse volume that obscures internal structures. Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can reproduce observed views but, under limited surgical view coverage, may distribute opacity through a thick and geometrically ambiguous band. We introduce height-field 2D Gaussian Splatting (H-2DGS), a three-stage pipeline that concentrates a robust 3DGS reconstruction, fuses its depth into a shared truncated signed distance field (TSDF) surface, and represents that surface with curved, surface-oriented Gaussian primitives. Separate height, color, and opacity bases provide local geometry and appearance, while a neighbor-transition objective coordinates overlapping patches. The explicit surface further supports postoperative alignment: MRI-derived depth deforms the reconstruction, and tracked-color supervision with alternating optimization preserves its appearance. Across five real neurosurgical cases, H-2DGS gives low multi-view depth inconsistency, a compact 7.97MB representation, and interactive rendering at 29--42ms per frame. The resulting sharp, deformable surface integrates clearly with tractography and MRI anatomy, including a postoperative resection cavity.

Graphics.title: HimmBO: High-Dimensional Interactive Model-Merging Bayesian Optimization for Image Generation
Graphics.summary: Fine-tuning has become a common way to customize text-to-image models, leading to community collections of over 100K lightweight adapters. Adapters sharing a base model can be merged with continuous coefficients. This turns a large collection into a high-dimensional continuous design space, which recent work explores interactively using preferential Bayesian optimization (PBO). However, existing approaches are limited to a few dozen preselected adapters and require expensive image generation in every interaction round. We introduce HimmBO, a two-stage method that scales preference-driven adapter merging to much larger collections while reducing image-generation cost. Its screening stage recovers the active adapter set through level-set estimation over pre-generated images, requiring no image generation. The refinement stage then optimizes merge coefficients in the recovered low-dimensional subspace. Both stages use a style-aware kernel, allowing preference information to transfer between visually similar adapters. In simulated-user image-matching experiments, HimmBO achieves higher final similarity than all comparisons while reaching a given similarity with under one tenth of the image generations required by prior work. Its performance remains stable as the collection grows to 1080 adapters, while competing methods degrade substantially.
